description:
The course offers a general view of the inorganic and physical fundaments of chemistry.
Part 1: A description of matter at the microscopic level, with an emphasis on atomic and molecular structure.
Part 2: The structure of solids, description of gasses and liquids/solutions, phase transitions. Introduction to the chemical
conversion of compounds, with an emphasis on acid-base and electrochemical reactions; the thermodynamic and kinetic
description of reactions and the origin of equilibria. Emphasis is repeatedly focused on the Lithium-ion battery, the fuel cell and
the production and storage of hydrogen.
learning_objectives:
Upon completion of the course, the student will recall the molecular structure of materials and is able to explain the relation
between atomic/molecular structure and macroscopic properties. The student is familiar with the elementary principles of
thermodynamics and reaction kinetics and is able to apply these to chemical reactions and equilibria, in particular with regard to
acid-base reactions and electrochemistry. Together with fellow students, the student knows how to study an inorganic subject in
depth and present the essentials in an oral presentation. The student can use Microsoft Excel for data storage, for the calculation
of inorganic and physic-chemical parameters and for the reproduction of simple functions.

description:
Calculus course with the subjects Complex numbers, Limits and differentiation, Integrate, Differential equations, Series, Vectors
lines and planes.
learning_objectives:
Complex numbers:
- The student can perform arithmetic operations with complex numbers, determine the modulus and argument of a complex
number, write a complex number as e-power and make a sketch of the complex number in the complex plane.
- The student can solve quadratic equations and determine the nth roots of a complex number.
Limits and differentiation:
- The student knows the concepts of limit, continuity, differentiability and differential.
- The student can determine limits by clamping, by distributing the main element, with the rule of the l'Hospital, and with Taylor
polynomials.
- The student can differentiate implicitly, and determine tangents to curves and linearisations of functions.
Integration:
- The student can calculate simple, indefinite and specific (single) integrals, if necessary by using: substitution, fractional splits
and partial integration.
- The student knows the (properties of) the inverse functions arcsin, arccos and arctan.
- The student recognizes improper integrals and can determine whether they are convergent or divergent.
Differential equations:
- The student can prepare a differential equation for some physical situations.
- The student can solve 1st-order differential equations by filling in an e-power, using separation of variables or by means of an
integrating factor.
- The student can approach the solution with the Euler method.
- The student can solve both homogeneous and simple inhomogeneous, linear 2nd-order differential equations with constant
coefficients.
- The student can describe solutions of the form A cos (omega t) + B sin (omega t) in the form C cos (omega t - alpha).
Series:
- The student can use the sum notation. The student knows the definitions of convergent and divergent rows and series. The
student can determine the limit of a convergent recursively defined row.
- The student recognizes geometric series and p series and knows when they are convergent or divergent. The student can
determine the sum of a convergent geometric series.
- The student can demonstrate divergence of series with the nth-term test and apply the integrated test to demonstrate
convergence or divergence.
- The student can approach a function with a Taylor polynomial and estimate the error at a certain interval.
Vectors, lines and surfaces:
- The student can add vectors and scalarly multiply. The student can calculate products, lengths, distances, angles and
determinants internally and externally. The student can calculate surfaces of triangles and parallelograms and volumes of
tetrahedra and parallelepipeda.
- The student can draw up an equation for a sphere with a center point and a radius, and can conversely (possibly split off with
squares) determine the center point and radius from an equation for a sphere
- The student can determine parameter representations of lines and planes, and with the aid of a normal vector determine an
equation for a plane.

description:
Fundamental concepts
Heat, work and internal energy
The importance of state functions
Thermochemistry
Entropy and the second and third law of thermodynamics
Chemical Equilibrium
The properties of real gasses
Phase diagrams and the relative stability of solids, liquids and gases

a. have knowledge of the basic concepts and laws of thermodynamics;
b. be able to qualitatively predict the behavior of simple thermodynamic systems on the basis of thermodynamic laws;
c. being able to do simple processes and systems based on the learned quantitative calculations
You should be able to answer questions such as:
What are the laws governing the behavior of an (ideal) gas?
What is the specific heat?
Why is it impossible to convert heat completely into work?
What is the energy available for work?
What is an adiabatic process?
What is a reversible process?
What is a Carnot cycle?
How to increase the efficiency of cycles.
Calculate the entropy, enthalpy and Gibbs energy or a chemical reaction and their dependence on temperature and pressure.
Determine the equilibrium constant or a reaction and its dependence on temperature and pressure.
What is the difference between real and ideal gasses?
How do you calculate the osmotic pressure?

description:
Concepts from coordination chemistry are explained on the basis of important applications of metals in nature, in medicine, in
materials or in homogeneous catalysis. These terms include: nature of coordination binding; coordination number, symmetry,
geometry and isomerism of complexes; 18-electron rule; stability and reactivity of complexes; spin states and magnetism;
oxidation states and redox chemistry, ligand field breakdowns and ligand field stabilization energy.
learning_objectives:
After passing the exam:
- the student is able to explain and apply the different aspects of coordination chemistry (including isomerism, jargon).
- the student can reason the ligand field breakdown of d-orbitals in different geometries.
- the student can make a judgment about the stability and reactivity of a random coordination connection.
- the student is familiar with important applications of coordination chemistry in, for example, medicine and catalysis.

description:

learning_objectives:
By the end of the course, students should be able to:
1. Recognize engineering roles in society.
2. Recognize the nomenclature of chemical engineering. Know systems of units and dimensions. Define and relate process
variables. Learn basic unit operations of chemical processes and describe how each works qualitatively.
3 (!!!). Use a systematic approach to solve chemical engineering problems. Identify variables, draw and label a process flow
chart from a word description. Perform and use degrees of freedom analysis. Formulate mathematical expressions that represent
word problems.
4. Work effectively in teams. Recognize the skills needed to function in a team. Write a clearly structured report.

description:
Functional groups, hybridization and orbitals. Delocalization and conjugation. Inductive effects and steric hindrance. Acids and
bases and their qualitative strength. Reactions of aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and derivatives and the corresponding
mechanisms. Aromaticity. Thermodynamics and kinetics of reactions, mechanisms.
Introduction to spectroscopic methods: UV-VIS, 13 C-NMR and 1 H-NMR, chemical shift, spin-spin coupling, IR spectroscopy
Stereochemistry and chirality. Enantiomers and diastereomers, racemic mixtures. Conformation analysis, Newman projection,
1.3 diaxilal interaction. Substitution reactions of aliphatic compounds and associated mechanisms. Nucleophilicity and leaving
group. Electron-sucking and driving substituents
Heteronuclear coupling, strong coupling in 1 H-NMR, Karplus relation, "high order" phenomena in NMR spectra, structure
clarification.
Elimination of aliphatic compounds. Stereo selectivity and stereo specificity. Electrophilic addition, the chemistry of enols and
enolates. Electrophilic and nucleophilic aromatic substitution. Conjugated addition. The corresponding response mechanisms.
NOE effects in NMR, two-dimensional NMR (1 H-1 H and 13 C-1 H correlated spectra). Dynamic effects in NMR.
learning_objectives:
Learning objective 1
Ready knowledge and application of functional
groups, the orbitals and their reactivity, fundamental concepts such as conjugation, aromaticity.
Learning objective 2
Insight into the mechanism of the most important reactions that the functional groups can undergo in terms of electron
movement and orbitals, acid and base strength, configuration and conformation
Learning objective 3
Skills in interpreting spectroscopic data of organic compounds. Insight into the relationship between the structure of organic
compounds and their spectra

- Running and standing waves
- Electrostatics
- Limitations of classical mechanics
- Basic concepts in quantum mechanics
- Schrodinger comparison solutions
- Particle in a box
- Quantum description of harmonic oscillator and rigid rotator
- Electron structure of atoms and simple molecules

mechanics, standing and running waves, oscillations and rotations and electrostatics
- The student knows the limitations of classical physics and can argue in which cases a
quantum mechanical description is needed

simple systems

description:
During this course a number of important biological molecules will be discussed from a (organic) chemical perspective. The
biosynthesis of amino acids, sugars, nucleic acids and lipids and their role in the biosynthesis and degradation of complex
biopolymers will be discussed. Certain complex biological processes, such as phosphorylating paths and post-translational
modifications will come to order. A broad frame of view will be made for each biological process. Zooming in, a set of specific
chemical processes and their mechanisms behind it will be discussed.

course_name: Chemistry and Physics of Solid Materials
description:
In this course the fundamental chemical and physical properties of solids and materials will be discussed.
We will start with how solids are built up by discussing the bonds between atoms. From there we continue with crystal
structures, Miller indices, the reciprocal space and Brillouin zones. Gradually we will look more and more at the properties of
materials that arise from their structure.
basic chemical and physical properties of solids and materials.
We will start with how solids are built up by discussing the bonds between atoms. From there we continue with crystal
structures, Miller indices, the reciprocal space and Brillouin zones. Gradually we will look more and more at the properties of
materials that arise from their structure.
Essential prior knowledge: chemical thermodynamics, quantum chemistry and physics, calculus 1 and 2, inorganic chemistry.
The following topics will be covered:
Theory of atoms and molecules, including the Bohr model and the quantum mechanical model, and the Schrödinger equation
Theory of solids, including connections in metals, tire structure, and electronic structure
Crystal structures, including X-ray diffraction and Miller indices
Transport properties of solids, including metals, insulators and semiconductors
Optical properties of solids
Diffusion in solids, including thermodynamics and kinetics
Mechanical, thermal and magnetic properties of solids
learning_objectives:
The student:
- Has an idea based on the atoms how a material is constructed, in terms of bonds and structure.
- Can understand the construction of molecules and materials based on quantum chemical aspects.
- Understands the basics regarding the presence of electronic bands in materials
- Can indicate how diffusion of ions in solids is influenced.
- Can discuss how thermal, mechanical and magnetic properties depend on the material composition.
- Can discuss the factors that influence electrical and optical properties of semiconductors and metals.
- Can make a selection of materials that are suitable for a specific application based on the above aspects

description:
The energy, recycling and safety course focuses on the safe and sustainable use of energy and raw materials. It consists of a
theoretical framework and teamwork (5-6 students per team).
Topics to be discussed are:
Energy:
- Relationship between availability of energy and prosperity / well-being
- World primary energy consumption, fossil energy
- Population growth; carrying capacity of the earth
- Earth energy balance, greenhouse effect, climate change
- The "Energy transition". Learning curves renewable energy technologies (PV, Wind etc), energy storage, material intensity
renewable energy
- "Renewable Energy for Industry (IEA)"
Recycling:
- Main classes of materials
- Plastics and recycling (application dependent, types of plastics)
- Biobased plastics (what can you do with them, what was the intention)
- The various types of reuse "downcycling", "recycling" & "upcycling" (lower, same, higher value after reuse)
- Aspects related to total fraction of fossil => polymers (approx. 5% max.10%, CO2 footprint)
- Design of products versus reusability (e.g. PET, nylon = OK, metallized laminate packaging film = NOT OK)
- Pro's and con's of polymers/plastics, replacement/alternatives, dilemmas, context in society
Safety:
-Introduction to risk and safety, conceptual framing and typing
-Risk Management: Safety history, legislation, risk management models, location-related risk calculation and group risk
-Process safety, safety in the process industry: what is specific to it, what are new trends? What are major accidents that have
been compromised and the lessons learned?
-Human and Organisational Factors of Safety (HOFS): Safety Culture (climate) and framing in performance management
-Risk Analysis Techniques: discussion, classification
Academic skills:
- written reporting (structure, structure and argumentation - report)
- teamwork
learning_objectives:
1. Knowledge
a. The student is familiar with the material covered in the themes of energy, recycling and safety and can answer questions about
this
b. The student is familiar with the way in which a report/article/publication must be set up.
2. Insight and understanding
a. The student is able to propose solutions for current issues
b. The student is able to develop new ideas
c. The student is able to model certain aspects.
3. Apply the substance
a. The student is able to apply the subject matter of the course to issues from current practice.
b. The student is able to make the correct assumptions for modeling the practical situation.
c. The student is able to work out a topic on an academic level in a team and to present this in a good (scientific or popular)
article/publication/report.

description:
The course physiological chemistry is concerned with biochemical processes in relation to diseases. The student will be taught
the molecular and cellular basis of acquired and inheritable anomalies in lipids, proteins, sugars and nucleic acids.
learning_objectives:
1. Knowledge
The student is familiar with the basic terms of physiological chemistry.
2. Insight and understanding
The student will be given insight into the cellular molecular processes engaged in: protein synthesis, control and degradation,
metabolism of lipids and sugars, hormonal regulation of metabolism and its connection to the brain, by using concrete examples.
3. Application and analysis
The student is capable of applying the taught material on questions and cases from physiological chemistry.

description:
Component Physical Chemistry:
Ideal and real solutions; electrolyte solutions (thermodynamics, activities); electrochemistry (Nernst equation, different kinds of
cells, fuel cells, batteries); transport (diffusion, migration); electrode kinetics (Butler-Volmer, kinetics and transport)
Component Kinetics:
Kinetic gas theory; elementary chemical kinetics: reaction rate equations based on elementary reactions, sequential and parallel
reaction steps, (perturbation of) equilibria and temperature dependence; kinetics of complex reactions: pre-equilibrium,
Lindemann mechanism, homogeneous, heterogeneous and enzymatic catalysis, radical reactions and explosions; the build up of
surface potentials, elementary molecular reaction dynamics. Complex kinetic processes are being actively studied by applying
the requisite mathematical models, with the aid of, e.g.: Excel and / or Maple. To this effect, each student receives homework
exercises.

description:
The Chemical Product Design course provides insight into the aspects that play a role in the development of chemical products.
Teams of 5-6 students work on designing a product. The goal is to effectively use the creativity and acquired knowledge about
chemical engineering of the team to develop an innovative but realistic new product.
The following topics are covered in the course:
-Working efficiently in a team
-Aspects that are important for product design
-The relationship between product properties and physico-chemical composition
-Development of physico-chemical models to describe product properties.
-Identifying customer needs
-Generating new ideas.
-Selecting the most promising idea.
-Developing a new product.
The course mimics the situation in a chemical company, where a new product is developed. Your team is a group of engineers
who have received this task from their manager. The role of the manager is played by a staff member of the Chemical
Engineering Department (the mentor).
learning_objectives:
1. General Skills
A. The student can work (creatively) in a team.
B. The student is able to report the results of the (team) work in writing, to present and to discuss orally.
2. Knowledge
A. The student is familiar with the basic concepts of product design.
3. Understanding
A. The student is able to indicate the relationship between physical-chemical properties and product properties.
B. The student is able to identify a new product.
4. Application and analysis of the content
A. The student is able to apply the content of the lecture in the field of chemical process/product technology.
B. The student is able to make a quantitative physico-chemical model of relevant product characteristics.
5. Synthesis and evaluation
A. Using the knowledge and skills acquired in this course the student is able to design new products.

-Dedication, motivation, enthusiasm, creativity
-Able to function in a (multicultural and multidisciplinary) team

-Able to report in writing and orally with attention to requirements for scientific communication and accountability
-Able to communicate effectively in Dutch and English, using modern presentation techniques

description:
This lecture series is a follow up of the first year course organic chemistry 1. A number of new reactions are introduced, such
that the student obtains a complete picture of the fundamental reactions and reaction mechanisms of organic chemistry: -
nucleophilic (aromatic) substitution; - electrophilic aromatic substitution; - elimination reactions;
- nucleophilic- and electrophilic addition; - cyclo addition; - radical reactions.
Both the conditions and the mechanisms of reactions, prediction of the reaction product and retro-synthetic analysis are treated in
this course. The specific subjects treated are:
- Diels-Alder addition; - Wittig reaction; - nitration; - diazotations; - Sandmeyer reaction; - reductive amination; - amino acids; -
pI calculation; - enzyme mechanisms, role of cofactors; - Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation; - alkylation of enolates; -
Dieckmann rearrangement; - hard and soft nucleophiles.

The Separation Technology course can be seen as the core of Chemistry: after each synthesis, one or more processes necessarily
follow to separate the product from by-products and residual reactants, solvents and other additives. This course deals with the
six most important separation processes, of which the first five tare based on phase equilibria.
1. Distillation
2. Extraction
3. Absorption
4. Adsorption
5. Crystallization
6. Membrane separations
Because thermodynamic phase equilibrium ultimately indicates which level of separation is aimed for by a system and moreover
indicates how much work is required as a minimum, the following thermodynamic topics precede the relevant separation
processes. And also, because modelling of chemical processes, requires a correct treatment of their thermodynamics, much
attention is devoted to the fundaments of the thermodynamics of following systems.
1. Phase equilibrium
2. Ideal and non-ideal liquid vapor equilibrium
3. Non-ideal liquid-liquid equilibrium
4. Crystallization, liquid-solid equilibrium
learning_objectives:
1. Knowledge
a. The student is familiar with the most important industrial separation processes and the thermodynamics of physical and
chemical equilibrium.
b. The student is familiar with the general recipe for drawing up mass and energy balances.
2. Insight and understanding
a. The student is able to interpret phase diagrams for ideal and non-ideal, reactive and non-reactive binary and ternary systems
based on thermodynamic information available in the literature and to prepare them where necessary. The student is capable to
describe aforementioneded systems thermodynamically.
b. The student is able to make a selection based on knowledge of basic principles.
c. The student is able to model the various forms of transport.
3. Application and analysis of the substance
a. The student is able to quantify the quality and yield of a separation process on the basis of the phase information provided.
b. The student is able to make the correct assumptions for modeling practical situations.
c. The student is able to quantify models from works, i.e. developing phase diagrams based on thermodynamic models and data,
calculating mass and energy flows, to be able to determine basic dimensions of separation devices.
4. Synthesis and evaluation
a. The student is able to apply the basic principles to new situations and to assess the plausibility of a certain choice on its
plausibility.
b. The student is able to prepare and assess the analysis of a (part of a) separation process and to
i. Method: the application of available theoretical or derived information;
ii. Numerical elaboration with the help of literature or experimental data;
iii. Plausibility of the accuracy and order of magnitude of the answers obtained.

description:
"Soft Matter" includes a class of materials from everyday life that exhibit characteristics of both liquids and solids. Such
materials are found in a large part of traditional chemical & food products as well as in high-tech applications ranging from nano
-medicine to energy.
This course offers an extensive overview of "soft materials", their properties, analysis methods and synthetic strategies and
explores the relationship between their structure, dynamics and properties. Moreover, the course also illustrates how their
properties can be used in traditional and high-tech chemical products.
The course starts with the chemical synthesis, molecular forces and principles needed to describe the elementary theories that
underlie the structure and dynamics of these materials. It then develops further into the description of their microscopic and
macroscopic properties. We will then examine how these quantities can be determined experimentally. The course deals with
systems such as polymers, surfactants, dispersions and liquid crystals and learns how the different types of molecular interactions
can be used in (advanced) applications
learning_objectives:
After successfully completing this course, students will be able to:
describe and discuss the properties of soft materials
calculate basic properties that characterize these materials
use elementary theories to describe the structure, dynamics and properties of soft materials
choose the appropriate characterization method for the evaluation of a certain characteristic
Understand and critically discuss basic concepts underlying the behavior of soft materials
to interpret quantitative experimental data
describe how molecular interactions and material structures can be used in an industrial application
propose molecular systems that are suitable for a specific application

description:
The course Statistical Thermodynamics and Spectroscopy comprises two parts:
- Statistical Thermodynamics (Edgar Blokhuis)
- Spectroscopy (Dennis Hetterscheid)
* As the name suggests, the first part on the Statistical Thermodynamics very much builds on the knowledge acquired in an
introductory course in Thermodynamics, but now we delve deeper in the underlying world of atoms and molecules and see that
all thermodynamics quantities, such as temperature or free energy, carry microscopic interpretation in terms of the movement of
molecules and atoms.
Chapter 1: a short review of Thermodynamics
Chapter 2: the link between Thermodynamics and Statistical Thermodynamics is discussed leading to a formalism that allows us
to calculate the free energy from all the available states of the system.
Chapter 3: The formalism derived in Chapter 3 is applied to the Ideal Gas. It is shown how Statistical Thermodynamics provides
a way to calculate equilibrium constants for chemical
reactions from spectroscopic data.
* Spectroscopy is a collective term for scientific techniques that investigate the interaction of matter with irradiation. In this part
of the course the general principles of spectroscopy are explained and the student will learn to correlate spectroscopic data with
the quantum mechanical description of the matter investigated, and vice versa. Main topics are: molecular symmetry, group
theory, atomic spectroscopy, UV/Vis spectroscopy, infrared spectroscopy and Raman spectroscopy.
learning_objectives:
Learning objectives for spectroscopy:
The student is able to determine the (most important) quantum states of a given material (atoms, small molecules) and can
assign these states to energy Terms.
The student is able to determine which quantum state(s) belong(s) to the ground state.
The student can rationalize which transitions between quantum states as a result of an absorption, emission or scattering event
have a more than zero probability of taking place.
The student can determine which atomic orbitals, molecular orbitals, vibrational normal modes and energy terms belong to a
particular irreducible representation and rationalize from there which transitions in vibrational and electronic spectroscopy are
symmetry forbidden.
The student is able to determine which vibrational motion belongs to a particular transition in the infrared region.
The student is able to qualitatively predict which signals are to be observed in the rotational, vibrational or electronic spectrum
of various materials ranging from single atoms (atomic spectroscopy) to large molecules (IR, Raman, UV-vis spectroscopy).

The classical theory of gravity can be interpreted as the geometry of space-time.It combines the language of field theory with the
language of differential geometry onmanifolds. The basic concepts of these subjects will be introduced and it will be shown how
they are used to describe gravitational phenomena, from relativistic corrections to orbits of planets and stars, to gravitational
waves, black holes and the evolution of the universe at large.
Topics:
Review of newtonian gravity
Review of Special Relativity
Differential geometry on manifolds, including the concepts of metric, connection and curvature
Equivalence principle, geodesic motion
Einstein equations, variational principle
Gravitational waves
Schwarzschild solution, stars and black holes
Cosmology of a homogeneous and isotropic universe
learning_objectives:
This course provides the basis for work in relativistic astronomy, cosmology, quantum gravity and applications. It will:
- acquaint you with the concepts of field theory and differential geometry
- teach you to use these concepts to solve problems of gravitational physics and cosmology
- prepare you for advanced courses on gravitational physics and cosmology
- allow you to access the scientific literature on these topics and understand the recent progress in experimental and
observational research

description:
This module deals with the fundamentals of Material science and of Mechanics of Materials.
Aerospace Materials is a course that teaches the fundamentals of material science needed for an understanding of the behaviour
of materials in a structure.
Aerospace Mechanics of Materials is, just like the Statics and Dynamics courses, part of the foundation of the mechanics on
which much of aerospace engineering is based.
The module is taught in two separate courses: Aerospace Materials and Aerospace Mechanics of Materials. Please see the course
description of the underlying courses for more details regarding the contents and set up of the course.
learning_objectives:
At the end of the module students will be able to independently solve problems related to Aerospace materials and Mechanics of
materials.
For more detailed learning objectives please see the learning objectives of the underlying courses.

description:
This course deals with the understanding of material properties and performance and how these are connected to basic structural
behaviour. This includes learning the reasons behind certain material properties and how to change some of them. Furthermore,
students will learn concepts as stresses and strain in tensile, shear or bending and how to apply these in basic structural elements.
Thermal properties and their origin will also be addressed. As durability of aerospace structures is crucial, also the corrosion
resistance and other degradation considerations will be discussed. Finally, the link between material properties and material
selection for design considering the environmental impact of materials production and use is made.
The course will cover the following aspects in an aerospace materials context:
-Material-related concepts such as elastic modulus, stiffness, plasticity, yield, ductility, strength, toughness, hardening, Tg, Tm,
thermoset, thermoplastic, elastomer, electrochemical potential, electrical/thermal conductivity
-Microstructure-dependent and microstructure-independent properties
-Material properties and their relation to material composition and microstructure
-Development and use of material indices for material selection in a given design
-Stiffness-limited design
-Strength-limited design
-Fracture-limited design
-Fatigue-limited design
-Materials behavior at high temperatures
-Materials degradation (corrosion, oxidation)
-Environmental considerations of the impact of material choice and use (circular economy)
-Strategic thinking to select materials for a target design

This course deals with understanding of basic structural behaviour. Students will learn about concepts such as stress and strain
under different kinds of loading (e.g. tensile, shear and bending).
Additionally, students will develop skills to solve statically indeterminate structural problems.
learning_objectives:
At the end of this course, the student will be able to:
Use mechanics to solve basic problems dealing with the stress/strain/displacement of structures in static equilibrium under
mechanical & thermal loads.
Use mechanics to solve basic problems dealing with the relation between material behaviour & structural behaviour under
mechanical & thermal loads.

learning_objectives: Basic understanding and overview of field of Aerospace Engineering.

description:
This first part of the course Introduction to Aerospace Engineering presents an overall picture of the aeronautics domain. This
overview involves a number of different perspectives on the aerospace domain, and shows some basic principles of the most
important concepts for flight.
Then the basic aerodynamics are covered, followed by flight mechanics.

performance

description:
This part of the course Introduction to Aerospace Engineering is focused on two aerospace disciplines: "spaceflight" and
"structures and materials". These topics are discussed in detail and will provide an understanding for both aircraft and space
missions.
learning_objectives:
- List/describe the reasons for going into space and the principles of rockets, including their trajectories.
- Motivate the selection of spacecraft configurations depending on the mission and identify the main elements of a satellite.
- Describe the features of the space environment and their consequences for space activities.
- Determine elementary satellite orbits, transfer orbits and maneuvers.
- Describe and work with elementary space propulsion aspects: launch, velocity budget and rocket equation.
- List the characteristics of typical aerospace materials & structures and describe their meaning and relevance.
- List the main structural elements of an aerospace vehicle and describe their functions and performance.

description:
This module consists of two courses:
AE1111-I Exploring Aerospace Engineering
AE1111-II Engineering Drawing

learning_objectives:
This module aims to apply the basic skills they will require to study aerospace Engineering:
- Learn to study at a university level.

description:
In your project groups of approximately 10 people you will be analysing the design of a flying wing for a mission on Mars.
During the project you will be asked to perform assignments related to the design of this wing including small experiments in
aerodynamics, flight and orbital mechanics. You will also design, build and fly a model of a flying wing.
You will develop your team working skills and reflect on them. You will be required to report your results after each session in a
small report and summarize the outcomes of your work in a scientific poster.
This project is related to the Introduction to Aerospace Engineering courses (AE1110).
learning_objectives:
At the end of the project you must be able to:
- explore the reasons behind the design of an aerospace vehicle
- apply the knowledge from the related courses
- work in small groups and reflect on your role within the group

description:
You will learn skills to register the geometry of engineering solutions. You will train professional sketching techniques by doing
assignments. You will get acquainted with the conventions for technical drawings and you will make computer based 3D models
and drawings of Aerospace related parts and assemblies.
The skills you learn will be used in the course of your education in projects and other assignments where the geometry of a
design needs to be documented.

At the end of this course, the student will:
1 Be able to sketch straight lines and fluent circles and ellipses.
2 Be able to use the ellipse rule for correct placement of circular and cylindrical items.

10 Be able to read and interpret engineering drawings.
Be able to use the 3DEXPERIENCE software for:
11 Making feature based parametric surface and solid models.
12 Making assemblies.
13 Making Detail and Assembly drawings compliant to the taught drawing conventions.
14 Collaboration on a group assembly.
15 Designing a multi-part assembly in a group context.

description:
This mentor programme is to support, stimulate and motivate first year students in starting university.
All first year students are assigned to a mentor group where different aspects of studying at Aerospace Engineering are
addressed.

description:
This module deals with the fundamentals of Engineering Mechanics: Statics & Dynamics.
It is a natural continuation from Newtonian Mechanics and laws of conservation of energy from high school. This module forms
the foundation of the mechanics on which much of aerospace engineering is based.
The module is taught in two separate courses: Statics and Dynamics. Please see the course description of the underlying courses
for more details regarding the contents and set up of the course.
learning_objectives:
At the end of the module students will be able to independently solve problems related to Statics and Dynamics by selecting the
appropriate solution method.
For more detailed learning objectives please see the learning objectives of the underlying courses.

description:
Statics deals with the principles of equilibrium. In this course, the principles of forces and moments will be explained as well as
principle of equilibrium of forces and moments. This also includes the equilibrium of 2D and 3D structures and trusses.
Furthermore the principle of internal forces and moments is addressed as well as the use of the principle of virtual work to
calculate both external and internal loads. Finally, the concepts of centre of gravity, centroids and moments of inertia are
discussed.
learning_objectives:
At the end of this course, the student will be able to solve basic problems dealing with statics. They will be able to:
- Define the basic terms in statics such as force, moment, body using the
appropriate units and notations
- Use Newtons 1st law to determine the reactions on 2D and 3D bodies and
particles in equilibrium
- Calculate the centroids and mass and area moments of inertia of elementary
shapes (including thin-walled structures)
- Calculate the normal forces in a truss structure
- Calculate and construct diagrams of the distribution of internal normal forces,
shear forces, bending moments and torsion moments as a result of external loading including distributed loads following a
standard definition and recognise when diagrams do not follow this definition
- Use the principle of virtual work to derive internal and external forces and
moments of structures and systems

description:
This course introduces the basic concepts of kinematics and kinetics that are necessary to understand, analyze and design a
variety of mechanisms and machines, such as airplanes, automobiles or satellites. Dynamics is concerned with the description
and analysis of the movement of particles and rigid bodies (kinematics) and the relations between kinematics and kinetics (mass
and forces). The course covers the equations of motion and derived methods of analysis, namely the work-energy relation and
the linear and angular impulse-momentum relations.
learning_objectives:
The goal is to provide the necessary knowledge, insight and skills to understand and quantify the motion of particles and rigid
bodies (kinematics) and the relation between forces and motion (kinetics).
At the end of this course, the student should be able to:
1. Calculate motion of a particle using three different coordinate systems (rectangular, n-t and cylindrical)
2. Calculate dependent motion between two or more particles
3. Calculate relative motion between two or more particles
4. Draw free-body diagrams and kinetic diagrams to represent the dynamic equilibrium of a particle using three types of
coordinate systems
5. Write the equations of motion for a particle using three types of coordinate systems
6. Solve the equations of motion of a particle for forces or accelerations
7. Apply the principle of work and energy to a particle or a system of particles
8. Calculate power and mechanical efficiency of a machine
9. Apply the principle of linear/angular impulse and momentum for a particle or a system of particles, using conservation of
linear/angular momentum when applicable
10. Calculate planar motion of a rigid body or system of rigid bodies undergoing pure translation, pure rotation and general
planar motion
11. Calculate dependent motion in rigid body systems
12. Calculate the mass moment of inertia for a rigid body and system of rigid bodies
13. Draw free-body diagrams and kinetic diagrams to represent the dynamic equilibrium of a rigid body using three types of
coordinate systems
14. Write the equations of motion for rigid bodies using two types of coordinate systems
15. Solve the equations of motion of a rigid body for forces or accelerations
16. Apply the principle of work and energy for a rigid body and system of rigid bodies, using conservation of energy when
applicable
17. Apply the principle of linear/angular impulse and momentum for a rigid body and system of rigid bodies, using conservation
of linear/angular momentum when applicable

description:
This module deals with an introduction to Aerospace design.
The module is taught in two separate courses:
1) A project: Design and Construction
2) A course: Aerospace Design & Systems Engineering Elements
learning_objectives:
At the end of the module students will be able to independently solve problems related to the design of aircraft and spacecraft.
For detailed learning objectives please see the learning objectives of the underlying courses.

description:
In the project, groups of approximately 8-10 students will act as a structural design team. In the first project assignment, you will
explore the properties of different materials and complete a preliminary design. In the second project assignment, you will design
a structure that will be tested with a limited number of design variables; the structure has specified dimensions and should be
able to sustain a specified load while minimizing the structural weight. In the final third project assignment, you will combine
the lessons learned from the first and second assignment and apply them to a new (structural) design problem with more
variables. Each assignment will have defined deliverables which need to be handed in before the stated deadlines during the
project.
A technical writing (TW) course runs concurrently with the project, but is scheduled separately. During the 5 TW sessions, you
will be taught how to write technical reports and improve your writing skills. TW is run by TPM faculty staff.
A Technical Writing Information Literacy (TWIL) course is part of the project. This (online) course will teach you searching for
relevant literature which is required to be incorporated into the Design Reports for each assignment. This course is part of
technical writing. This course is run by TU Delft library staff.
Information with respect to course logistics, relevant deadlines and project assignments will be communicated using the
Brightspace course page.
Note: First year students are automatically enrolled and assigned to a (new) group. Upper year students who did not complete
the Design and Construction project please contact Education-AE (Education-AE@tudelft.nl) to be registered before February
1st.
learning_objectives:
At the end of the project you will be able to:
- Independently complete a full design cycle of an AE (sub)system
- Performing a complex team project under external guidance and reflect on its outcome
- Write an effective design report

description:
This course addresses the design of aerospace systems in general and more in particular the preliminary design of airplanes,
spacecraft and rocket launch vehicles.
The following topics are addressed:
Aerospace design:
- Design process (in general and with application to airplanes, spacecraft and launch vehicles)
- Role of SE in the design process
- Functional & operational analysis, requirements generation
- Design concept selection & description (set up of trade off process)
Airplane design:
- Design requirements
- Preliminary weight estimation
- Preliminary sizing of wing area and engine power/thrust
- Analysis of aircraft configurations
- Fuselage design
- Wing and propulsion system design and integration
- Empennage and undercarriage design and integration
Spacecraft design:
- Spacecraft mission, main functions, main requirements, vehicle concepts
- Preliminary sizing of the spacecraft subsystems: 1) structures & mechanisms, 2) thermal control, 3) electrical power generation,
4) propulsion, 5) attitude determination and control, 6) command and data handling and 7) telecommunications
Launch vehicle design
- Launch vehicle mission, main functions, main requirements
- Launch vehicle concepts
- Single- and multi-staged launch vehicles
- Preliminary sizing of rocket stages and launch vehicle subsystems
The material treated in this course will be applied in later thematic projects (BSc year 2) and the Design Synthesis Exercise (BSc
year 3). Follow on courses are scheduled in year 2 and 3 of the aerospace engineering bachelor curriculum.
learning_objectives:
At the end of this course, the student shall be able to:
- Identify and explain the aircraft/spacecraft architecture and the conceptual design process.
- Identify and explain aircraft and spacecraft missions
- Perform a simple functional analysis and generate a list of requirements
- Generate a conceptual aircraft design and perform a preliminary sizing of the aircraft (wing, fuselage, empennage,
undercarriage)
- perform a preliminary design & sizing of the most important spacecraft and space launch vehicle subsystems including the
subsystems structures and mechanisms, thermal control, electrical power generation, propulsion, attitude determination and
control, command and data handling and telecommunications
- Perform a simple trade-off

description:
The course is based on the chapters 14-31 of the book Physics for Scientists & Engineers (with Modern Physics), Fifth Edition,
Pearson, by Douglas C. Giancoli. For the course Pearson made a customized edition called "Thermodynamics, waves and
electromagnetism" containing these chapters only.
Waves part (chapters 14-16):
- simple harmonic motion, energy of harmonic motion, simple and physical pendulum, damped harmonic motion, forced
oscillation (resonance)
- wave motion (transverse and longitudinal), energy transported by waves, wave equation, superposition, reflection,
transmission, interference, refraction (Snell's law), diffraction, standing waves (resonance)
- sound, sound level (decibel scale), vibrating strings and air columns, quality of sound, noise, superposition, interference (beats),
Doppler effect
Thermodynamics part (chapters 17-20):
- temperature, thermometers, thermal equilibrium, zeroth law of thermodynamics, thermal expansion, gas laws (Boyle, Charles
and Guy-Lussac), absolute temperature, ideal gas law, ideal gas temperature scale (triple point), Avogadros number
- kinetic theory of gases, molecular interpretation of temperature, Maxwell distribution of molecular speeds, real gases and
changes of phase, critical temperature, phase diagram, triple point, vapor pressure and humidity, Van der Waals equation of
state, mean free path, diffusion (Ficks law)
- heat as a transfer of energy, internal energy (of ideal gas), specific heat, calorimetry, open, closed and isolated systems, latent
heats, first law of thermodynamics, work, state variables, work done for isothermal, adiabatic, isobaric and isovolumetric
processes, molar specific heat of a gas (at constant pressure and constant volume), principle of equipartition of energy, equation
of state for adiabatic expansion/compression of an ideal gas, heat transfer by conduction, convection and radiation (Stefan-
Boltzmann law)
- Clausius statement of the second law of thermodynamics, heat engines, Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law, reversible
and irreversible processes, Carnot cycle, Carnot efficiency, Otto cycle, heat pumps, refrigerators and air conditioners (coefficient
of performance), entropy and why it is a state variable, general statement of the second law of thermodynamics (in terms of
entropy), order and disorder, statistical interpretation of entropy (Boltzmann formula), microstates and the macrostate of a
system, third law of thermodynamics, thermal pollution, energy resources and global warming
Electromagnetism part (chapters 21-31):
- electrostatics, Coulomb's law, electric field, electric dipole, electric flux, Gauss's law, electric potential, equipotential surface,
capacitance, capacitors in series and in parallel, electric energy storage, dielectrics
- electric battery, electric current, resistance (Ohm's law), resistors is series and in parallel, electric power, DC circuits,
Kirchhoff's rules, RC circuits
- magnetism, force on electric current and electric charge in magnetic field, torque on a current loop, magnetic field due to
straight wire, Ampères law, Biot-Savart law, magnetic materials, electromagnets
- electromagnetic induction, Faradays law, Lenz's law, electric generators, transformers
- mutual and self inductance, electromagnetic oscillations, AC circuits containing resistance, inductance and capacitance
(resonance), impedance matching
- above mentioned laws of electromagnetism are revisited in the form of Maxwells equations, Gauss's law for magnetism
- electromagnetic (EM) waves as solutions of Maxwells equations, light as EM waves, EM spectrum, speed of light, Poynting
vector, radiation pressure, wireless communication
learning_objectives:
At the end of this course the student will be able to use physics to solve basic problems from science and engineering (and in
particular aerospace engineering) related to thermodynamics, waves and electromagnetism.

description:
The module AE2111 consists of the project AE2111-I (System Design) and the course AE2111-II (Aerospace Design and
Systems Engineering Elements II)
For detailed content please consult the individual parts of the module
learning_objectives:
The module aims at teaching students to identify, analyze and design aerospace (sub)systems and to report this newly acquired
knowledge either as an individual by taking an exam, doing a test or presenting it with visual aids or as part of a group by
working on a design and handing in work package reports.

description:
The theme of the project is System Design. As a subject of this project, teams work on either the design of a spacecraft, or the
design of an aircraft wing. This project is supported by a course on 'Oral Presentations'.

General Subsystems
a. What are the vehicle subsystems and how do they function and interact?
Key Subsystems
b. How to design an operational reliable spacecraft communications system and an ADCS system?
c. How to determine the wing geometry according to the aerodynamic requirements? How to design the high lift devices and the
ailerons of an aircraft? Which Class II weight estimation methods are available, and how can they be used?
learning_objectives:
1. Identify vehicle subsystems and understand their functionality
2. Analyze most important subsystems
3. Design top-level subsystems including their operations
4. Identify some of the main subsystems of Aircraft and Spacecraft and explain their functions
5. Describe Space flight control lay-outs and Attitude Determination and Control System (ADCS) designs and show their
functionality
6. Understand how to estimate the lift and drag characteristics of both an airfoil and a wing.
7. Understand the conceptual sizing approach of aircraft high lift devices and ailerons
8. Understand how to estimate the weight of each aircraft component through Class II weight estimation methods
9. Explain and apply basic rules to design and size a spacecraft communications system

description: Subsonic and Supersonic Aerodynamics + Wind tunnel practical
learning_objectives:
Obtaining a good knowledge in the fundamentals of aerodynamics and its relevance to and application in the aerospace
technology domain

description:
Derivation of basic flow equations
Fundamental concepts of fluid flow
Potential flows in two and three dimensions; elementary solutions
Airfoil and wing theory for inviscid, incompressible flow
Determination of lift and induced drag of finite wings
learning_objectives:
At the end of the course the student should be able to:
1.Explain aerodynamic concepts and apply aerodynamic theory for incompressible flows.
2.Apply the fundamental concepts of mechanics to describe fluid flow
3.Derive the governing equations that are valid under general conditions (viscous, compressible flow)
4.Describe the relevance of different flow regimes (compressible/incompressible, viscous/inviscid)
5.Describe and apply the aerodynamic concepts that are used in the description of flows (streamlines, circulation, vorticity, etc.)
6.Explain the essential phenomena that occur in incompressible flows in relation to the generation of forces (lift, drag)
7.Calculate the lift and pressure distribution over airfoils using potential theory (thin-airfoil theory)
8.Indicate the effects of viscosity on the behavior of airfoils
9.Apply lifting-line theory and VLM for calculations of wing lift, lift distribution and induced drag
10.Apply the airfoil & wing theory in a wind tunnel experiment

description:
1) Measuring the properties of a two-dimensional airfoil and a three-dimensional wing in a low speed windtunnel
2) Pressure measurements, wake measurements and demonstration of flow phenomena.
3) The measurement results are compared to basic CFD calculations on the spot.
learning_objectives:
1) Illustration of some of the topics adressed in the course ae2110
2) Getting acquainted with the real flow conditions (e.g. effects of viscosity) over a 2 airfoil and 3D wing
3) Illustration of the restricted accuracy of basic CFD approaches for wing aerodynamics

description:
How to apply the basic laws of mechanics and thermodynamics to describe compressible flows?
What are the essential phenomena that are relevant and specific to aerodynamic behaviour under compressible flow conditions
How to apply the theory in the prediction and computation of compressible flows (airfoils, engine intakes, nozzles)
learning_objectives:
At the end of this course, the student will be able to:
1. Understand aerodynamic concepts and apply aerodynamic theory for compressible flows.
2. Explain which essential phenomena occur in compressible flows and explain the relevance of different flow regimes
(transonic, supersonic, hypersonic)
3. Apply the fundamental equations of fluid mechanics and thermodynamics to describe compressible flows; derive the
governing equations for compressible flow
4. Calculate the flow through channels and nozzles.
5. Calculate the flow properties of airfoils in supersonic flows (linearized theory, shockwave-expansion theory).
6. Explain the effects of viscosity on the behavior of airfoils in compressible (transonic) flow.
7. Describe the basic steps towards non-linear supersonic flow.
8. Perform a supersonic flow experiment and calculate basic shock wave properties.

description: Structural Analysis, Design, and Vibrations
learning_objectives:
Being able to design and analyse a structure with respect to:
Bending
Buckling
Torsion
Shear
Cutouts
Castigliano's second theorem
Vibrations

description:
The following topics will be addressed in the course
a) Unsymmetrical Bending,
b) Stress function solution for torsion
c) Torsion of thin walled open and closed sections
d) Shear of thin walled open sections (shear center)
e) Multi-cell structures (bending, shear, torsion)
f) Structural Idealization - Sheet-boom approximation / Multi-cell beams
g) Cutouts and Reinforcement Ribs
h) Energy Methods
i) Buckling
learning_objectives:
At the end of this course, you will be able to:
(a) Calculate stresses/strains in thin walled structures using:
- engineering beam theory (bending and shear)
- torsion theory (closed and open sections)
(b) Modify above theories in the presence of cutouts and/or taper
(c) Calculate displacements using:
- beam theory
- energy methods (Castigliano's theorems)
(d) Determine buckling loads for simple structures (beams, trusses)
(e) Design such structures where you determine the geometry so that structure does not fail
(thickness of skins under bending, shear and torsion; cross-sectional geometry of beams under compression)

description:
Aerospace structures are commonly subjected to vibrations during operation. This includes harmonic loads as found in low and
high-speed rotating equipment or impact loads due to collissions. For analysis and design purposes it is critical to model the
response of a structure under free and forced loading conditions. This course is an introduction to vibrations in structures and
covers the following topics:
1. Introduction to vibrations and modelling of structures.
2. Free vibrations of undamped, single degree-of-freedom systems
3. Free vibrations of damped systems
4. Harmonically-forced vibrations
5. Vibrations under general loading types: impulse loading, step loading, arbitrary transient loading.
6. Modal analysis: Free vibrations of undamped multiple degrees-of-freedom systems
7. Forced vibrations and damping in multiple degrees-of-freedom systems
Fundamental concepts of structural vibrations are introduced in the course, such as discretization of kinematical and force
connectors, choice of degrees of freedom (DOF), lumped mass approach, damped and undamped natural frequencies, resonance,
critical, undercritical and overcritical damping, transfer function.
learning_objectives:
General course aim:
The purpose of this course is to provide an introduction to vibrations of structures and structural components. At the end of the
course, students should be able to analyze basic vibration problems and be able to use this information for design purposes.
Learning outcomes:
Students who successfully complete the course should be able to
1. Represent an actual structure or structural component using a mass-damper-spring model.
2. Formulate and solve the equation of motion associated to the mass-damper-spring model.
3. Understand the influence of the main model parameters on the structural response.
4. Interpret the results of the simulations in terms of global cases such as resonance and under or over-damped responses.

course_name: Applied Numerical Analysis and Computational Modelling
description:
This module introduces the foundations of numerical analysis and computational modelling. See the descriptions of AE2220-I
and AE2220-II for detailed content lists.
learning_objectives: See the descriptions of AE2220-I and AE2220-II

description:
Applied Numerical Analysis (Weeks 1-7, Dr. R.P. Dwight)
_____________________________________________________________
A foundational course in numerical analysis. We assume good knowledge of real analysis and calculus, but no previous
experience in numerical analysis. We introduce numerical methods for solving non-linear equations, ODEs, optimization
problems and integrals. We analyze these in detail, with regard to consistency, accuracy, stability and convergence, theoretically
and in practice.
1. Taylor Series and Solutions of non-linear equations.
- Computer arithmetic and round-off errors.
- Concepts of accuracy, consistency, stability and convergence.
- Uses and limitations of numerical methods.
- Solution methods for non-linear equations:
2. Polynomial interpolation
- Statement of the interpolation conditions.
- Important properties of polynomials, the Weierstrass approximation theorem.
- Choice of basis: monomial, Newton, Lagrange.
- Uniqueness and existence of polynomial interpolants.
- Gibbs phenomena.
3. Advanced interpolation methods and regression
- Interpolation on triangles and rectangles (patches).
- Splines.
- Radial basis functions and volume splines.
- Least-squares regression
4. Numerical differentiation and integration
- Finite difference formulas, truncation error, rounding error.
- Quadrature based on polynomial interpolation.
- Derivation of integration conditions.
- Newton-Cotes and Gauss rules
- 2D integration based on product rules.
5. Numerical methods for solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs)
- Properties and classification of ODEs, standard form of ODE.
- Definition of a consistent ODE solver.
- Linear stability analysis (von Neumann analysis), time-step criteria.
- Convergence analysis.
- Single and multistep methods:
6. Numerical optimization
- Define the unconstrained optimization problem
- Local and global optima, design space, cost function, derivatives.
- Quadratic forms as an example problem.
- Common optimisation methods
learning_objectives:
At the end of this part of the course, the student should be familiar with:
1. The Taylor Series and Solutions of non-linear equations
2. Polynomial interpolation
3. Advanced interpolation methods and regression
4. Numerical differentiation and integration
5. Numerical methods for solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs)
6. Numerical optimization

description:
Complex physical phenomena, from flows to structural deformations, are often modelled using partial differential equations
(PDEs). This course provides an introduction to the numerical solution of PDEs . We begin by describing the general principles
of computational modelling, and investigate the properties of PDEs derived from common physical problems. We then describe
two popular discretisation approaches, the finite-difference and finite-element methods, along with techniques used for their
analysis and practical application. In the last part of the course, we consider time-march methods for unsteady problems, and
basic iterative techniques for the solution of large algebraic systems.
1. Introduction to computational modelling
- Errors in the numerical representation of physical phenomena
- Requirements for discretisation methods
2. Classification and boundary conditions
- A review of model PDEs
- Basic classification of PDEs
- Definition of characteristics, Elliptic, hyperbolic and parabolic PDEs
- Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions, well-posed problems
3. Finite-difference methods
- Modified equation, Taylor table
- Upwinding and artificial dissipation
- Generalised transformation
- Fourier analysis
4. Verification
- Method of manufactured solutions
- Code and solution verification, Richardson extrapolation.
5. Spectral and finite-element methods
- Method of weighted residuals
- Element and global assembly
- Application of boundary conditions
- Unsteady problems
6. Analysis of time-march methods
- Accuracy of transient computations
- Systems of ODEs, semi-discrete eigenvalues
- Wave space, relation to Fourier analysis
- Fully-discrete eigenvalues, stability, stiffness
7. Iterative solution of algebraic systems
- Direct solution methods versus iterative solution methods
- Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel techniques
- Convergence rates, stopping criteria
learning_objectives:
At the end of this part of the course, the student should be able to:
1. Select appropriate numerical discretisation techniques for a given PDE
2. Formulate physically consistent numerical boundary treatments.
3. Analyse numerical discretisations in terms of their accuracy and stability.
4. Select a time-march method well-suited to a given problem.
5. Understand the design and behaviour of iterative solution techniques.
6. Verify the results of numerical simulations

description:
This module contains two courses, AE2235-I, Aerospace Systems and Control Theory and AE2235-II, Instrumentation and

description:
This course teaches the elements of handling dynamics in systems encountered in Aerospace Engineering. The goal is to provide
students with all the theory and tools necessary to enable them to design, implement, and operate control systems for aerospace
systems. An important part of the course is the actual programming (in Python/Matlab) of control systems for a wide variety of
aircraft, UAVs, and satellites. For this, the student is introduced to the concepts of dynamical systems; inputs, outputs and
system boundary and environment. Students learn to connect different system descriptions; state-space models, transfer
functions, differential equations and frequency response descriptions. Students learn block diagram descriptions and block
diagram manipulation. Desirable and undesirable properties of control systems are distinguished, the choice between elementary
controller types to match a specific controlled system is discussed. Tuning methods for the controller parameters include the root
-locus method, and frequency design methods (Bode).
The course uses examples commonly found in aerospace engineering, both dynamic models for whole systems (aircraft or
satellites) and models for components, such as a landing gear or control surface with a hydraullic servo.
learning_objectives:
At the end of this course, the student will be able to:
1. Given a schematic of a physical system and desired behavior, design a simple (single-loop) controller.
2. Formulate linear dynamical system models from block diagrams or schematic mechanical system descriptions.
3. Identify dynamical properties across domains time, frequency, transfer function, A-matrix eigenvalues.
4. Evaluate stability of open and closed loop systems (in different domains: time, frequency, on the basis of pole locations)
5. Calculate and judge responses to input signals in time and frequency domain.
6. Select appropriate controller from basic types (P, PI, PD, PID, lag-lead, lead-lag) depending on system properties and
requirements.
7. Tune controllers with Bode, Nyquist and Root-locus methods (Evans) with a computer.
All the above tasks will be done using a Computer Aided Control System Design (CACSD) tool, in this case either Matlab or
Python.

description:
Week 1, Lectures 1-2
Introduction; Basic principles of signal acquisition, conditioning, modulation and transfer;
Definitions (continuous time, discrete time, periodic/a-periodic); Basic signal shapes (unit pulse, step, ramp, sinusoid); Refresh
complex algebra, Euler's theorem;
Introduce Unit impulse function (Dirac, sifting property)
Week 1, Lectures 3-4
Signal decomposition; Fourier Series (real and complex exponential versions); Sinc function; Examples.
Week 2, Lectures 5-6
Fourier Transform, Basic Transforms, Duality, Transform pairs, Properties of FT, Convolution; Examples.
Week 2, Lectures 7-8
Relation Fourier Transform and Fourier Series; Examples
Energy and Power, Parseval's Theorem; Definition of Energy and Power Spectral Density; Examples.
Week 3, Lectures 9-10
Introduction to linear time-invariant systems (LTI); Impulse response function, Transfer function; Examples.
Week 3, Lectures 11-12
Fourier Analysis, Frequency-response function; Filtering, filtering properties (bandwidth, rise time); Examples.
Week 4, Lectures 13-14
Sampling; A/D and D/A conversion; Impulse-train sampling and signal reconstruction; Nyquist sampling theorem, aliasing;
Examples.
Week 4, Lectures 15-16
Introduction to Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) and Fast-Fourier Transform (FFT); Examples
Week 5, Studio Classroom Session
Sampling, aliasing, windowing, leakage. Basic signal conditioning; Basic filter design: Low-pass, High-pass, Band-pass. Using
data from actual aerospace sensors.
Week 6, Lectures 17-18
Basic principles of transferring information (communication); modulation (digital system, binary signaling); On-Off-Keying, and
Binary Phase Shift Keying; Time and frequency representation.
Week 6, Lectures 19-20
Effects of noise; Additive White Gaussian Noise (AWGN); thermal noise, noise temperature, noise density, effective noise
bandwidth; Signal-to-Noise-Ratio (SNR); Signal detection.
Week 7, Lectures 21-22
Optimal signal detection (false alarm and missed detection probabilities); range estimation for navigation and surveillance;
examples in aerospace; signal bandwidth versus bit-rate (communication) link/channel capacity, and bit energy to noise density
ratio Eb/N0. Signal bandwidth versus ranging accuracy (navigation), chip/pulse duration, and carrier to noise density ratio C/N0.
Week 7, Lectures 23-24
Design calculations for telecommunications sub-system in aerospace; basic radio (wireless) signal link budget (aand radar
equation): Emitted Isotropic Radiation Power (EIRP), free space
loss, and antenna gain. Examples: satellite-Earth link, aircraft-tower link, and radar two-way sensing; quick review of transmitter
and receiver building blocks.
learning_objectives:

description:
Please note: up to date information about the exchange programme will be published on the Brightspace page Student Exchange
Programmes Aerospace Engineering.
During the Bachelor programme you have the possibility to follow the 30 ECTS of your Minor programme abroad at one of the
partner universities that the Faculty of Aerospace Engineering has an agreement with. The Faculty of AE has a number of places
for allocation under the semester exchange agreement with the partner university, either bilateral, or as part of a TU wide
agreement. Please be aware that even though there is an active agreement, this doesnt mean there are exchange places available
every year. An overview of exchange partner universities can be found at: lr.tudelft.nl/exchange.
Usually you need to create a free minor course package, which means you make your own selection of courses that meet the
requirements of the partner university and the requirements of the TU Delft Faculty of Aerospace Engineering. Students are
encouraged to choose a Minor outside the field of Aerospace Engineering.
The Minor abroad in academic year 2023-2024 needs to meet the following criteria:
1. It is possible to complete the Minor abroad in one semester.
2. The proposed Minor has to be a coherent set of courses, which match preferably one or maximum two themes. The theme can
be related to the field of Aerospace Engineering or a completely new field, however the courses cannot have overlap with the
content already provided in the Aerospace Engineering BSc and MSc curriculum. For the approval of the courses, a strong
argumentation must be made which shows that the content of the courses are interrelated and clearly represent the chosen
theme(s). This argumentation, in the form of a motivation letter, must be submitted with your Minor abroad application.
3. The Minor is composed of 3rd- and, if applicable, 4th-year BSc courses of at least 15 ECTS. It is allowed to take a maximum
of 15 ECTS from 2nd year BSc courses, or 1st year courses if well motivated, to close a gap in pre-knowledge in fields other
than Aerospace Engineering. MSc courses are allowed if well motivated.
4. A (research/course) project with a maximum of 10 ECTS is allowed, as long as it is in line with criteria 2 and 3 and can be
registered as a course on the transcript of the partner university.
5. With reference to criteria 3, the Minor is allowed to contain a maximum of 6 ECTS of cultural courses that relate to the host
country OR language courses in the language of the country of the partner university. This is to support your integration into the
host country. These 6 ECTS are not part of the 15 ECTS 3rd- or 4th-year courses. English or a language that the student is
already proficient in is not allowed to be taken as a language course.

description:
The Design Synthesis Exercise (DSE) students are required to make a design in the field of aircraft, spacecraft or wind turbines.
In the design project the student is provided with an opportunity to obtain "design experience". This means that the student goes
through the complete design process, from drawing up a set of detailed (mission) requirements, concept analysis and design,
concept selection to the presentation of the final design, in a structured and iterative manner.
He/she will experience the difficulty of making well-motivated design choices, thereby taking into account (sometimes
conflicting) demands, etcetera. He/she will also experience that design iterations are necessary to tune non-optimal design
decisions to meet the specifications drawn up at the start of the exercise. Some examples of aerospace vehicles designed in the
past include:
High-altitude VTOL rescue
Thin Haul Transport and Air Taxi
Water Bomber UAVs
Aircraft Maintenance Drone
Returning to Saturn - Characterizing the Icy Moons and Rings
Demonstrator for Airbreathing Electrostatic Propulsion, Earth Observation Satellite
A Personal Air Mobility Vehicle as Maritime Pilot Shuttle
A stratospheric balloon as operational and test platform for Earth observation.
eVTOL emergency aircraft
Develop of a secondary rotor wind turbine
Low-cost system for stratospheric aerosol injection
Adaptive Regional Airliner
The credits that can be gained by successfully completing the exercise are 15 EC.
Students who have suggestions for design topics can bring them forward to the responsible instructor. The idea must be within
the topics of aircraft, spacecraft or wind turbine design and concern the design of a complete object. Parts of these objects,
mission designs without hardware components or procedures are not considered suitable for the DSE. If the idea seems feasible,
a suitable principal tutor will be sought. When a suitable principle tutor can indeed be found the text of the assignment can de
written and put forward to the external quality control committee.
Together with this principal tutor the student can draft the assignment. The assignment will have to pass the regular quality
control procedure. If successful, the assignment will be offered to all the participants of the DSE in either the Spring of the Fall
DSE. The topic of the design is limited to aircraft, spacecraft or wind turbines. Participation of those that have helped with the
set-up of the design assignment is limited to two students per design team.

- Technical competence and ability to apply knowledge

description:

- Verification of the numerical model against existing (analytical) models.
