description:
In het vak DP1 Diving into Design duiken studenten in het ontwerpen en gaan ze 3 ontwerpuitdagingen aan. Tijdens de duik
krijgen studenten inzicht in de 6 hoofdcompetenties van het ontwerpen navigeren, framing, concepting, visualiseren &
prototypen, evalueren en integreren - en zetten ze de eerste stappen in het aanleren van de vaardigheden die daaraan gekoppeld
zijn. Zo beginnen ze aan de klim om vanuit een bewuste onbekwaamheid, bekwaam te worden in het ontwerpen.
Daarnaast beginnen studenten in DP1 aan hun eigen professionele ontwikkeling (onder de noemer IDME) waarmee ze
uiteindelijk in staat zijn om zich te ontwikkelen tot de soort ontwerper die ze willen worden. De eerste stap hierin en de focus
voor deze ontwikkeling in DP1, is het leren studeren en begrijpen dat je als student zelf verantwoordelijk bent voor of en hoeveel
je leert.
De focus van DP1 ligt op het aanleren van het iteratieve ontwerpproces en de stappen van de ontwerpcyclus daarin. Zo gaan
studenten in meerdere iteraties erop uit om te begrijpen waarvoor en wat ze moeten ontwerpen, hoe ze dat kunnen ontwerpen
door veel ideeën te genereren en deze ideeën te schetsen, bouwen en 3D modelleren, en of dat wat ze ontwerpen in de praktijk
doet wat het zou moeten doen. Hiervoor passen studenten aangereikte methodes toe en kennis uit de parallelle vakken
Understanding Product Engineering, Understanding Humans en Understanding Organisations om een ontwerp te ontwikkelen
waarin rekening is gehouden met zowel werking en constructie, functionaliteit en gebruik, als vorm en uitstraling. Het leren
ontwerpen is hiervoor gericht op iets tastbaars wat redelijk dicht bij de belevingswereld van de studenten. Het uitgangspunt voor
alle projecten is het ontwerpen van een fysiek product voor een gegeven organisatie en doelgroep.
learning_objectives:
Als studenten het vak afgerond hebben, kunnen ze:
1. een eigen studeerstrategie formuleren, met behulp van feedback kritisch reflecteren op de uitvoering ervan en hun eigen
handelen daarop aanpassen (5.1.1, 5.1.3, 5.4.3)
2. aantonen dat ze aangereikte methodes voor de verschillende stappen van de ontwerpcyclus in meerdere iteraties kunnen
toepassen (1.1.2),
3. laten zien dat ze de context van een gegeven ontwerpkader vanuit de perspectieven mens, organisatie en technologie kunnen
verkennen in een iteratief proces (1.3.1),
4. demonstreren dat ze vanuit een gegeven ontwerpkader een oplossingsruimte in de breedte kunnen verkennen (1.4.1),
5. door het maken van simpele schetsen, prototypes en 3D modellen demonstreren dat ze kunnen reflecteren op hun eigen
ontwerp en het ontwerp verder kunnen ontwikkelen (1.5.1),
6. beoordelen of hun ontwerp voldoet aan het ontwerpkader door experimentele testen uit te voeren (1.6.1),
7. aantonen dat ze rekening houden met verschillende ontwerpaspecten (de werking en constructie, de functionaliteit en het
gebruik, de vorm en uitstraling) in de conceptontwikkeling van een ontwerp (1.2.2).

description:
Om producten in de fysieke wereld te ontwerpen moet een ontwerper de technische basisprincipes kennen van het product en
zijn onderdelen. Een gestructureerde technische analyse van bestaande producten is daarbij nodig om deze kennis beter te
begrijpen en toe te passen in een toekomstige ontwerpcontext.
Er bestaat een overweldigend aanbod aan materialen en productieprocessen, maar ook aan analysemogelijkheden om te
voorspellen hoe producten (gaan) functioneren in verschillende situaties. Om wegwijs te worden in dit veld wordt de student
geïntroduceerd in vijf technische aspecten van tastbare producten, namelijk: Functie, Productarchitectuur, Materialen,
Productietechnieken en Modellering, gerepresenteerd in het zogenaamde Techniekwiel.
In dit vak staat het product centraal, van waarlangs het techniekwiel wordt doorlopen. Naast de functie van alle onderdelen in het
product en de relatie tot elkaar, zal ieder onderdeel worden geanalyseerd op de meest voorkomende materialen en
productietechnologieën. Daarnaast zal door middel van een systematische analyse van geometrie, uitwendige en inwendige
belastingen, en de leer van spanningen en vervormingen de student inzicht krijgen in de technische haalbaarheid van onderdelen
in de productarchitectuur.
Dit vak legt de relatie uit tussen materiaalgroepen en hun belangrijkste eigenschappen, de belangrijkste verschillende
productieprocessen die daarbij gebruikt worden, en de kansen en beperkingen die dit biedt voor productontwerp. De student
maakt kennis met deze aspecten door het routineus verkennen van een tastbaar product, het te begrijpen door middel van analyse
en abstractie, en het te evalueren op de vijf aspecten van het Techniekwiel.

Design shapes the world, as much as the world co-shapes design. But what is design? In order to understand what constitutes
Industrial Design Engineering, we need to find out what vocabulary, practices and methods are commonly used here in Delft and
around the world. What shifts in the triangle of technology, society, and economy have co-created designs vocabulary, practices,
and methods? How have shifts in our understanding of consumption shaped the field? How have shifts in production co-
constituted what design is now? How to situate seemingly newfangled terms like complexity and systems thinking?
Understanding the history of the present field of design future-proofs students: it will ready them for the next iteration of the
field.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course you will be able to:
1.(cid:9)Recognize and explain through concrete examples how design, society and culture influence each other (2.8.1, 2.8.2)
2.(cid:9)Recognize and contextualize the field of designs vocabulary, practices, and methods in relevant historical developments (3.1.1)
3.(cid:9)Critically reflect on knowledge, information, and common sense, and towards the domains of design and society (5.1.1.)

description:
In this introductory course students are asked to look at organisations from three different interests:
1.(cid:9)a technical interest with a lens focusing on efficiency/control and cause/effect,
2.(cid:9)an interpretative interest with a lens focusing on the life experience of people in a cultural and organisational context,
3.(cid:9)a critical interest with a lens focusing beyond the status quo.
Students will learn about key scholars, typical persons for each of these interests. Students will apply their knowledge of interest
one and two by reporting on contemporary organisations by paying attention to the shaping of organisations, setting innovation
goals, organising innovation, business economics, brands and organisational types & structures. Students will work with the third
interest by devising a design brief while paying attention to ethics.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
1.(cid:9)distinguish between different types of innovation and analyse how these are related to design within organisations (LO 2.9.3).
2.(cid:9)distinguish between different types of systems and explain different types of behaviour of these systems (LO 3.2.2).
3.(cid:9)identify the organisations capabilities, the brand values and network relations in the current context (LO 2.9.1).
4.(cid:9)explain a basic business case based on estimated revenues and costs for a new design of a product-service system (LO 2.10.5).
5.(cid:9)apply knowledge of the variety of business models to develop an inclusive and sustainable product-service system that
supports global prosperity (LO 3.3.4).
6.(cid:9)apply the principles of effective learning to collaborate in a project (LO 6.2.1)
7.(cid:9)identify social issues in design and acknowledge the professional responsibilities of designers (LO 3.4.1).
8.(cid:9)analyse the ethical values of a design challenge and use these as inspiration for design brief development (LO 3.4.2).
9.(cid:9)morally explain design brief decisions and to discuss ethical issues in a design context (LO 3.4.3).

description:
In de cursus Understanding Humans staat de mens centraal en wordt hierover design-relevante kennis aangeboden. De cursus
geeft een introductie in het waarom, hoe en wanneer mensen relevant zijn voor ontwerpers. Op deze basiskennis zullen de andere
vakken en met name de people electives in Semester 4 voortborduren.
We zullen 3 human kennis domeinen langsgaan:
Human Factors (met fysieke-, perceptuele-, en cognitieve ergonomie);
Human Experience (met emoties, esthetica, betekenis, motivatie en gedrag);
Human Context (met culturele-, sociale-, politieke context, en de context van het dagelijkse leven).
De Vitruvian Man zal het leidende karakter in het vak zijn. Hij zal zich steeds beter laten begrijpen en problematiseren.
learning_objectives:
2.6.1 Students are able to explain design-relevant factors of the human body and mind, including bodily functioning, the
perceptual system, and information processing.
2.6.2 Students are able to explain design-relevant factors of human experience, including emotions, aesthetics, and meaning.
2.6.3 Students are able to explain design-relevant factors of human motivation and behaviour, focusing on the internal and
external factors that influence human behaviour.
2.8.1 Students are able to explain design-relevant factors of cultural, sociological, political, economic and everyday-life contexts
that stage and shape social interactions.
4.1.1 Students are able to assess the value of different types of research and their outcomes.
4.1.2 Students are able to assess the value of different sources of information/ knowledge.
5.1.1 Students are able to express critical reflect their own thinking, decision making and actions and adjust these accordingly,
and reflect critically toward the domain.
5.2.1 Students are able to understand, justify, value, develop and explain theoretical arguments.
6.3.3 Students are able to present research and design outcomes clearly and convincingly in writing, verbally and visually.

description:
Digitale technologieen heeft een grote impact op nagenoeg alle sectoren van onze economie. Ze dragen bij aan de ontwikkeling
van innovatieve ontwikkelingen, zoals nieuwe producten, platforms en services. Ook andere manieren van waarde ontwikkeling
onstaan, zoals nieuwe klant ervaringen (customer experiences). Organisaties doen er vaak goed aan om digitale technologien in
hun korte- en lange termijn strategien op te nemen.
Het doel van dit project-gebaseerde vak is om studenten lean innovatie methodes toe te laten passen voor een bestaande
organisatie. Dit bedrijf heeft bepaalde zaken die ze goed doen. Vanuit hier gaan de studenten op zoek naar een manier om
nieuwe impact te maken in de levens van mensen. Niet alleen voor de klanten, maar voor de verschillende stakeholders die
betrokken zijn bij deze waardecreatie.
Dit vak is ook een platform voor studenten om eerder opgedane (theoretische) kennis toe te passen, zoals hun kennis over design
research, digitale producten, interaction design en het begrijpen van wat waarde is voor verschillende stakeholders.
Het vak bestaat uit 3 fases.
1. In het eerste deel gaan studenten individueel de behoeftes van de gebruikers onderzoeken in de context van waar het bedrijf
actief is. De uitkomst zal uiteindelijk een concept product-service systeem zijn.
2. In het tweede deel gaan studenten in teams van vijf één concept doorontwikkelen middels de lean startup methode. Ze zullen
in 3 sprints aannames op desirability, viability en feasibility proberen te valideren.
3. In het derde en laatste deel gaat de student individueel de waarde van het uiteindelijke concept onderzoeken. Hierin analyseert
hij/zij de waarde voor verschillende stakeholders en werkt zij/hij een passend, duurzaam business model uit.
learning_objectives:
Als studenten dit vak hebben afgerond, zijn ze in staat om:
LO1: een project te plannen en om een agile innovatie process te managen om een mvp te maken (1.1.3)
LO2: verschillende belangen van de stakeholders af te wegen om een haalbaar, wenselijk en levensvatbaar ontwerp met een
optimale impact te creëren (1.2.2)
LO3: het ontastbaar te laten zien en buiten de gebaande paden te treden ten behoeve van innovatie (1.4.3)
LO4: visualisaties, modellen en prototypes te maken voor het effectief beoordelen van een concept (1.5.3)
LO5: experimenteel te testen welke ontworpen functies/uitkomsten van het concept het bedoelde effect hebben (1.6.1)
LO6: de belangrijkste trends op het gebied van technologie, organisatie en mensen te analyseren en dit toe te passen in hun
concept (3.1.3)
LO7: om de uitkomst van onderzoeken en experimenten te gebruiken tijdens het ontwerp process (4.3.3)
LO8: onderzoek, experiment en design output op een duidelijk, onderbouwde manier te communiceren, zowel in schrift, verbaal
als visueel (6.3.2)

description:
This course provides students with the technical foundation to design and develop innovative digital products.
Students develop the ability to specify technical requirements such as Internet Architectures, database models and software
behavior. They leverage this understanding to apply the business model canvas, select the appropriate development methods and
reflect on their digital responsibility as designer.
Throughout the course, students navigate the seven dimensions of the product canvas. It is the compass to grasp the dynamics of
digital products and acquire the ability to effectively converse in a design and development process to realize digital products
that are technically feasible and commercially viable.
Students develop a hands-on understanding of core digital technologies and software development methods through Python
programming, and apply techniques and practices for iteratively creating, validating and improving digital products.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
1. explain core concepts related to the realization of digital products, such as technical architecture, networks, databases,
software development methods, business models, web technology and digital responsibility (2.5.2, 2.4.1, 2.4.3, 2.10.2)
2. specify algorithms and data structures driving the behavior of a digital product through pseudo code and UML diagrams
(2.5.2)
3. read and write basic Python code to prototype a digital product (2.4.1)
4. analyze and evaluate the technical aspects (code, data, network) and business aspects (canvas) of a connected product (2.4.3,
2.10.2)

description:
In Research for Design leren studenten over de waarde van onderzoek en wetenschappelijke kennis voor het ontwerpproces. Ze
leren hoe ze bestaande kennis kunnen toepassen in het ontwerpproces en hoe ze zelf onderzoek kunnen opstellen en uitvoeren
om nieuwe kennis te verkrijgen voor het ontwerpproces. Meer specifiek leren studenten hoe de verschillende fasen in het
ontwerpproces vragen om verschillende onderzoeksbenaderingen. Studenten leren hoe ze onderzoeksvragen moeten opstellen,
geschikte onderzoeksmethoden kunnen selecteren, gegevens kunnen verzamelen, analyseren, interpreteren en presenteren en, op
basis van de resultaten, implicaties voor het ontwerp en het ontwerpproces kunnen definiëren.
Tijdens Research for Design maken de studenten ook kennis met de verschillende onderzoeksthema's op de faculteit, door
middel van de opdrachten, voorbeelden en gastsprekers. Een gedeelte van de geleerde onderzoeksvaardigheden wordt toegepast
in Design Project 2 dat parallel aan dit vak loopt. Na dit vak zijn studenten in staat belangrijke onderzoekstermen te begrijpen,
zelf ontwerp-gericht onderzoek op te stellen en uit te voeren en onderzoeksresultaten te integreren in het ontwerpproces.
Studenten leren tevens om rekening te houden met ethische overwegingen bij het uitvoeren van onderzoek.
learning_objectives:
Als studenten het vak hebben afgerond kunnen ze (getal tussen haakjes verwijst naar het leerdoel van de complete lijst
eindtermen, waarvan het afgeleid is):
LO1: de kwaliteit van verschillende soorten onderzoek en de resultaten ervan beoordelen (4.1.1)
LO2: de kwaliteit van verschillende informatiebronnen en kennis beoordelen (4.1.2)
LO3: adequate onderzoeksvragen formuleren (4.2.1)
LO4: passende onderzoeksmethoden selecteren en toepassen om de onderzoeksvragen te beantwoorden (4.2.2)
LO5: zowel kwantitatieve als kwalitatieve onderzoeksgegevens verwerken en analyseren, en hieruit conclusies trekken voor het
ontwerp (4.2.3)
LO6: rekening houden met ethische overwegingen van onderzoek (4.2.4)
LO7: onderzoeksresultaten evalueren en reflecteren op generaliseerbaarheid en ontwerprelevantie (4.3.1)
LO8: onderzoeksresultaten adequaat presenteren, rapporteren (in tekst en beeld) en bediscussiëren (4.3.2)
LO9: onderzoeksresultaten toepassen tijdens het ontwerpproces (4.3.3)
LO10: kritisch reflecteren op hun eigen denken, besluitvorming en handelen, en deze aan te passen (5.1.1)
LO11: relevante argumenten voor hun ontwerpbeslissingen ontwikkelen en overtuigend presenteren (5.2.2)

description:
Understanding value(s) is a mandatory course which provides bachelor students with fundamental knowledge about the notions
of value(s) and what they mean for a broad range of stakeholders. They will learn to identify the values that are important for all
stakeholders involved in a new product-service system. They will learn to map-out these values, but also to analyse and explain
possible tensions. Specifically, students will learn to understand how a value proposition can create value for the intended users,
and how the organisations involved in putting this design on the market can capture economic value or revenue and therefore be
viable. Importantly, students will learn to look at the consequences and externalities of a design. Societal and ecological value(s)
will be scrutinised with a view to minimise harm and possibly increase benefits for indirectly affected stakeholders. In order to
attend to value tensions emerging in design projects, students will get knowledge to better reflect on design decisions and
outcomes using different ethical lenses. Eventually, students will be able to explain value flows in complex systems and to make
a more desirable value proposition for all stakeholders.
Through theoretical lectures and application in cases from practice in group projects, students will each week acquire knowledge,
methods and skills that will enable them to incorporate ethics and stakeholder value(s) into their design process. The knowledge
acquired in Understanding Values and the individual code of ethics that students will craft during the course will be relevant for
all design projects in following courses as well as in a design career.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
1 - Students are able to distinguish between different notions of value
2 - Students are able to set up a value proposition for an intended user (2.10.3)
3 - Students are able to acknowledge the effect of design on human behaviour and reflect on how a design outcome promotes or
hinders human values (2.6.3)
4 - Students are able to identify how an organisation intends to create and capture value (2.10.2)
5 - Students are able to identify relevant stakeholders for a new design and map the value flows to show what the value for each
stakeholder is (2.10.1)
6 - Students are able to identify social and ecological issues in design and acknowledge the professional responsibilities of
designers by assessing the value captured, missed and destroyed for both direct and indirect stakeholders (3.4.1)
7 - Students are able to ethically reflect on design challenges (3.4.2)
8 - Students are able to morally justify design decisions and to discuss ethical issues in different settings (3.4.3)

description:
Om interactieve producten te ontwerpen moet een ontwerper de basisprincipes van mens-machine interactie kennen. Deze
principes worden verzameld uit drie vakgebieden: (1) de psychologie voor het begrijpen of bedenken van de gebruikers ervaring,
(2) het ontwerpen voor vormgeving van interface en dynamisch product gedrag en (3) de electronica voor het kennen van
componenten en programmeren van een computer om deze componenten te laten samenwerken in de beoogde functie van het
product.
Voor kennis over het begrijpen en bedenken van de gebruikers ervaring wordt voortgebouwd op het vak Understanding Humans.
In Digital Interfaces wordt die kennis verdiept voor toepassing bij mens-machine interactie.
Het ontwerpen van mens-machine interactie is als het ontwerpen van een theater-stuk met verschillende scenes waarbij de
ontwerper vanuit de eerste persoon alle stappen van de gebruiker en de machine moet plannen, uitdenken en in de tijd achter
elkaar zetten. Het omhelst zowel de vormgeving van de productvorm als de choreografie van het dynamisch gedrag.
Voor kennis over de interactieve technologie wordt voortgebouwd op het vak Understanding Product Engineering en Digital
Product Design. In Digital Interfaces wordt de anatomie van een product-service system behandeld waar het gaat om het meten
van gebruiker acties (met sensoren), het schrijven van de software om de metingen om te zetten in een gewenste product reactie
(met actuatoren).
learning_objectives:
Als studenten het vak afgerond hebben, zijn ze in staat om:
LO1 principes van menselijke ervaring toe te passen, waaronder multi-sensorische esthetische ervaringen, zingeving en emoties
om een product-service systeem te ontwikkelen (2.6.2).
LO2 principes van vorm, inclusief vormeigenschappen en ervaringsaspecten, toe te passen om een product-service systeem te
ontwikkelen (2.7.2).
LO3 de principes van dynamische gedragskwaliteiten, fysieke betrokkenheid en zingeving toe te passen om een product-service
systeem te ontwikkelen (2.7.1).
LO4 kennis over sensorische waarneming toe te passen voor het ontwikkelen van een interactief product-service systeem dat de
omgeving en de mens waarneemt en daarop feedback geeft (2.4.2).
LO5 kennis van interactieve technologie, inclusief elektronische basiscomponenten, sensoren en actuatoren, en ingebedde
systemen toe te passen in de verwezenlijking van een ontwerp (2.3.1).

description:
In dit project maken studenten kennis met de complexiteit van het ontwerpen van producten en diensten (interventies) in
complexe netwerken (systemen) van organisaties, producten, diensten, omgevingen en gebruikers. Ze worden er van bewust
gemaakt hoe de introductie van, of een verandering in een product implicaties kan hebben op maatschappelijk, organisatorisch en
individueel menselijk niveau. Ook leren studenten hoe je daar als ontwerper grip op kunt krijgen.
Het project heeft als rode draad het toewijzen van de onderwijsruimtes verspreid over de verschillende faculteiten van de TU
Delft campus.
Als gevolg van de toenemende, dynamische vraag naar onderwijsruimtes bij de verschillende faculteiten van de TU Delft, staat
de TU voor de complexe uitdaging de over de faculteiten verspreide onderwijsruimtes op een efficiënt manier toe te wijzen. Er
zal gezocht moeten worden naar een systemische oplossing voor het toewijzen van onderwijsruimtes, passend bij onderwijsvorm
en verwachte aanwezigen, en rekening houdend met zaken als: de tijd die nodig is om van faculteit A naar faculteit B te komen,
financiën en korte-termijnbeschikbaarheid. De universiteit zou graag het thema mobiliteit als uitgangspunt zien en wil daarin
zoeken naar duurzame oplossingen voor het zich van A naar B verplaatsen over de campus. Er wordt begonnen met een analyse
en een eerste prototype, op basis waarvan de oplossing verder ontwikkeld wordt. Maar ook zullen andere richtingen verkend
moeten worden. Denk daarbij bijvoorbeeld aan een digitaal platform voor het reserveren van zalen, real-time toewijzen van
zalen, verplaatsen van faculteiten, enzovoorts.
Als system intervention designer zul je je eerst vertrouwd maken met het systeem van toewijzen van onderwijsruimtes aan de TU
Delft. Dat doe je door individueel in een systeemanalyse (4 weken) onder andere te bepalen wie de betrokken actoren zijn
(studenten, docenten, universiteit, facility management) en hun ervaringen met het gebruik van dit systeem in kaart te brengen.
Je focus zal liggen op een duurzaamheidsanalyse van de mobiliteit, terwijl je jezelf ook open stelt voor andere
ontwerprichtingen.
In teamverband zul je vervolgens in drie iteraties (12 weken) gaan ontwerpen. Die iteraties zijn er op gericht interventies
uitgaande van mobiliteit te verkennen en dan te beslissen of je daarmee doorgaat of dat je beter andere richtingen kunt
onderzoeken. Daarbij zul je van je oplossingen ook de impact op duurzaamheid laten zien vanuit natuur en milieu, sociaal en
economisch perspectief.
Tenslotte zul je in de laatste 4 weken reflecteren op een interventie die door een ander team ontwikkeld is. Je zult die interventie
zorgvuldig analyseren, suggesties doen voor verbeteringen en er ideeën uit halen die je kunt toepassen in je eigen interventies.
In de weken 4 (einde van de eerste, individuele opdracht), 8 en 12 (einde van de eerste twee ontwerpiteraties) zullen er ook
IDME-activiteiten zijn. Die activiteiten zullen er op gericht zijn om vanuit je design identiteit en je individuele en teamdoelen te
reflecteren op de genomen ontwerpbeslissingen en de verkende ontwerprichtingen.
learning_objectives:
Als studenten het vak afgerond hebben, zijn ze in staat
1. om geschikte procesmodellen, methoden en technieken te selecteren en deze keuze te onderbouwen voor het uitvoeren van een
iteratief ontwerpproces. (LO 1.1.1.)
2. om op verschillende abstractieniveaus te werken voor het creëren van een ontwerp dat een duurzame impact heeft op het
milieu, de maatschappij en de economie. (LO 1.2.1.)
3. om zich een mogelijke toekomstige context met betrekking tot een bepaalde situatie voor te stellen, met als doel een gewenste
toestand te formuleren. (LO 1.3.2)
4. om concepten te genereren die passen bij een gegeven ontwerpdoel. (LO 1.4.2)
5. om visualisaties, modellen en prototypes te maken voor het effectief testen en evalueren van hun concepten tijdens het
ontwerpproces. (LO 1.5.3)
6. om uitspraken te doen over de verwachte duurzame impact van een ontwerpresultaat op het milieu, de maatschappij en de
economie. (LO 1.6.4)
7. om een systeemperspectief te ontwikkelen voor verschillende ontwerpuitdagingen. (LO 3.2.1)
8. om complexe probleemsituaties te doorgronden door het onderzoeken van systemische patronen, relaties tussen stakeholders
en de variabelen van het systeem waarin het complexe probleem zich voordoet. (LO 3.2.3)
9. om maatschappelijke vraagstukken in het ontwerpen te identificeren en de professionele verantwoordelijkheden van
ontwerpers te erkennen. (LO 3.4.1)
10. om relevante argumenten voor hun ontwerpbeslissingen te ontwikkelen en overtuigend te presenteren. (LO 5.2.2)
11. om effectieve communicatiemiddelen te genereren voor verschillende doeleinden. (LO 6.3.1)

description:
This course is about DATA and specifically about using data as a design material. What does this mean? Well, we will teach you
with a basic understanding of what data is, the different types of data available, its particular qualities, ways of working with it,
and how you can use it in your design projects. Many products nowadays use and work with data in their functioning. Think
about digital services, devices within the internet-of-things but also robots need data to function. Data is further becoming
increasingly important as business intelligence and in the governance of cities. Therefore it is not surprising that design
approaches emerge that work with data. Examples are data enabled- or data-centric design. Data is thus all around, as an
invisible reality that affects us all, and requires design competence to work with data effectively and responsibly.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
LO1. explain how data can be used in the design process for understanding, inspiration, creation and validation. (3.2.2)
LO2. explain how data connects people, things and organizations in human activities that meaningfully binds them. (2.10.1,
2.10.3)
LO3. explain how to make data models by describing data as entities, attributes and relationships. (2.4.4)
LO4. explain how to develop a data collection strategy by identifying, comparing and selecting appropriate data sources. (2.4.3)
LO5. identify and consider both the merits and risks of working with data in the design process. (3.4.1 , 5.1.1)
LO6. explain how to use data visualisation effectively for discovery and communication purposes. (2.7.2)
LO7. identify and compare complex data analytical techniques and learn to perform a simple data analysis. (4.2.3)
LO8. identify and describe interaction mechanisms and qualities unique to data-driven products and services. (2.7.1)

description:
Thinking critically and creatively about the future is an essential part of every successful design process, but what are the best
ways to do this? In this course students will learn various methods of what is termed futuring imagining future designs, contexts,
and publics.
Students will discover the historical origins and cultural importance of futures thinking, encounter different types of design-
relevant futuring techniques, and reflect on the usefulness, limitations, and ethics of applying futures thinking in different design
contexts.
The course will include three interrelated components:
1. A survey of the historical origins and the social and cultural value of futures thinking.
2. Introduction to a variety of relevant futuring techniques.
3. Opportunities to consider and reflect on the application of futuring techniques in a variety of design spaces and situations.
learning_objectives:
Upon successfully completing this course, students will be able to:
1. Demonstrate a sensitivity for the impact of culture on design.
2. Envision a relevant future context for an organisation or a product-service system on organisation, human and technology
aspects.
3. Analyse the most important developments and trends regarding technology, organisation and people.
4. Formulate the implications of the analysis in previous LO for envisioning futures.
5. Identify the professional responsibilities of designers within the context of envisioning futures.
6. Assess the value of different types of research and their outcomes.
7. Demonstrate the ability to stay updated in the field of design.

description:
In Sustainable Impact, students learn about sustainability from the perspectives of People, Planet & Prosperity. They develop an
understanding of and learn methods for:
1. The complexity and interrelatedness of the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
2. How to translate the SDGs into practical priorities for their own design projects using systems thinking.
3. Quantifying environmental impacts using life cycle assessment (LCA).
4. Recovery strategies for products and materials.
5. Sustainable business models and Product Service Systems.
6. Energy effectiveness in products.
7. Influencing user / consumer behavior for sustainability.
The content of this course is relevant for students because environmental and social considerations are increasingly crucial for all
human endeavors, especially manufacturing, design, and business.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course, students will be able to:
LO1 - Explain the environmental & social concerns in the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) (LO 3.3.2, 3.3.3, 3.3.4)
LO2 - Identify social issues in design and acknowledge the professional responsibilities of designers. (LO 3.4.1, 3.4.2, 3.4.3)
LO3 - Prioritize sustainability concerns & solutions in your own design projects by applying systems thinking methods or tools.
(LO 3.3.1, 3.3.2, 3.3.3)
LO4 - Calculate environmental impacts using life cycle assessment (LCA). (LO 2.2.2, 3.3.2)
LO5 - Assess more sustainable materials & manufacturing methods using LCA, Granta CES Edupack, or other tools. (LO 2.2.2,
3.3.2)
LO6- Identify and ideate recovery strategies for products and materials. (LO 3.3.2, 3.3.3)
LO7 - Apply sustainable business models and Product Service Systems to make material recovery strategies economically
viable. (LO 2.10.2, 3.3.2, 3.3.3)
LO8 - Identify opportunities for energy efficiency, effectiveness, and sustainable energy production. (LO 3.3.2)
LO9 - Apply persuasive design tools to drive user / consumer behavior for sustainability. (LO 2.6.3)

description:
This course deals with the ability of design to counteract complex global and social challenges in domains such as elderly care,
mobility, mental healthcare, safety or biodiversity. There is an increasing demand for such social designers who are by hired by
governments, public and social sector organisations and other industries that want to make a positive impact on society.
In the course designing for society, you will learn how designers can make an impact in tackling complex societal challenges by
meaningfully shaping concepts that address both individual and societal concerns. To achieve this, the course uses the Social
Implication Design methodology (Tromp & Hekkert, 2018) as a framework to structure your design approach. The core of this
methodology is the development of a vision and design statement that are used to (re-) frame the challenge you are working on,
and that guide the development of concepts. In the course we will pay particular attention to the role of insights into experience,
meaning and behaviour in a design process. As such, the course combines gathering deep insights into human needs and
aspirations, with broad insights into implications for society and the planet.
To learn a design approach based on the social implication design methodology, this course divides the approach into four
phases, each aligned to one of four assignments:
Phase one is focused on an exploration of the domain at hand from an experiential and meaning perspective. Who are relevant
actors (people) in the domain? which current experiences are relevant to consider? and what values and meaning underlie these
experiences? In an individual assignment, you will learn to create a tangible probe that you can use to explore these phenomena.
In phase two, you will form groups in which you will combine the insights from phase one and complement these insights with
other context factors to work towards a future context and a design statement which explains how you intend to create change
through your design. The future context and design statement collectively make up your design vision.
In phase three, you will continue individually to develop and visualize a concept that is in line with your design statement, and to
develop an accompanying design rationale.
In the final phase, you will develop and build an experiential prototype of one of the concepts developed in your team, to test the
assumptions that were part of your design rationale. You will also anticipate and visualize the social implications of your design.
In addition to learning a new design approach in this course, you will be introduced to the practice of social design, and you will
reflect on the role you want to play as a designer in society.
learning_objectives:
LO 1: Students are able to deal with ambiguity and uncertainty during the design process in order to make decisions (1.1.4.
Ambiguity and uncertainty)
LO2: Students are able to systematically explore the context of a given design challenge from different perspectives to build a
clear understanding of the design challenge at hand (1.3.1 Explore design challenge)
LO3: Students are able to express critical reflection on their own thinking, decision making and actions and adjust these
accordingly, and reflect critically towards the domain (5.1.1 Critical thinking)
LO4: Students are able to create visualizations, models and prototypes to effectively reflect in action to develop the design (1.5.1
communicating concepts)
LO5: Students are able to balance different interests and concerns to develop a design with optimal sustainable impact that is
feasible, desirable and viable (1.2.2 Balance interests)
LO6: Students are able to identify social issues in design and acknowledge the professional responsibilities of designers (3.4.1
Moral sensitivity)
LO7: Students are able to envision a possible future context related to a given situation to formulate a desired state (1.3.2
Envision)
LO8: Students are able to identify and prioritise specific elements of the context to reframe a given proposition and formulate
realistic goals (1.3.3 Reframe)
LO9: Students are able to work effectively in teams (6.2.1 Work in teams)
LO10: Students are able to generate concepts that meet the design goal at hand (1.4.2 Generate concepts)
LO11: Students are able to generate effective communication means for various purposes (6.3.1 Communication means)
LO12: Students are able to make statements about the anticipated sustainable impact of a design outcome on environment,
society and economy (1.6.4 Anticipate impact)
LO13: Students are able to position themselves in the field of design (5.3.2 Position yourself)

description:
Brands define and differentiate organisations, drive performance and even shape the marketplace. In this elective students will be
introduced to the fundamental concepts in brands and branding. They will find out how brand managers cultivate a brand
position that resonates with consumers and sets them apart from competition, how brands can inform innovation and how design
brings value to the process of branding. They will learn about the strategic and tactical decisions brand managers face in building
and managing brands to maintain relevance and fuel growth.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
LO1. Determine and motivate the positioning of a new brand in relation to opportunities in the market (extending LO2.9.1).
LO2. Select, motivate, and develop brand touchpoints to realise the desired brand positioning for a new brand (extending
LO2.10.3).
LO3. Appraise possible management and innovation options for the brand to propose, motivate and elaborate a meaningful way
to fuel brand relevance and growth (extending LO2.9.4).

description:
The Business Model Design elective is a course on business models specifically developed for design students. It provides
bachelor students with an understanding of what business models are, how they can be designed and what the challenges and
opportunities for business model design are. Starting with business models at the firm level, the course will gradually move to
business models at the level of an entire ecosystem. Through working on a business model design challenge from practice,
students will acquire new knowledge, methods and skills that allow them to meaningfully engage in business model design
activities in diverse situations, including new ventures, creative studios and networks of organizations. The business model
design knowledge, methods and skills will be instrumental for the projects that students will execute in following courses (such
as design projects and master courses in strategic design (Design Strategy Project, Design Roadmapping, New Product
Economics)) and for determining the role they wish to have as a (strategic) design professional.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
1. Recognize and explain BM definitions and components.
2. Distinguish between different business model archetypes (deepening LO2.10.2)
3. Construct clear arguments for choosing a particular business model design and business model design method.
4. Identify relevant components for a new business model design, and map the value flows to show what the value for each
stakeholder is (deepening LO 2.10.1).
5. Construct a business model design for a firm, an interorganizational project, and ecosystem using existing methods.
6. Reflect on critical aspects of business model designs and formulate a statement that addresses or solves a business model
design challenge in a particular context.

description:
This elective course provides an understanding of the service design process with an emphasis on codesign. Different types of
organisations, whether in private, public or third sectors, are looking to codesign approaches as a way to design better services
that can meet human needs, while distributing benefits and burdens across society in equitable ways.
Codesigning services calls for a different way of doing things. Instead of designing 'for' people, its about designing 'with' people.
Also, designers must acknowledge that peoples experiences of services can be cocreated by multiple stakeholders interacting
through various types of service interfaces, such as rented products, environments and interpersonal encounters.
In this course you will study the fundamental concepts and theories about service codesign, learn to identify opportunities to use
service codesign in tackling organisational challenges, and apply codesign methods for the creation of new services experiences.
You will put knowledge into practice, working in teams to conduct codesign sessions with invited groups of participants. And
you understand the empowering role that professional designers can have in service codesign and learn to be more democratic in
the making of design decisions.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students should be able to:
1. Explain service codesign concepts and theories in a professional way. (LO 3.1)
2. Identify opportunities to address real-world challenges through service codesign. (LO 1.3)
3. Apply codesign methods to empower people in the creation of new services. (LO 6.1)

description:
In this elective course the students knowledge of human factors and ergonomics (HFE) is deepened. The HFE discipline takes a
human-centered and scientific approach to the design of products, services, and systems in a way that balances system
performance and human well-being. This course will guide students in acquiring knowledge on the complexities of the human
system in terms of physical, perceptual, and cognitive capacities. These capacities will provide the fundamental boundaries that
form the design space in which one can be creative. The course will provide the theoretical backgrounds in the human systems,
how the capacity of this system can be measured, and how these measurements can be used in a systems approach to the design
of product-service systems. Case studies will be in the field of healthcare, mobility, sports and consumer product design.
The following topics are covered:
1. Physical, perceptual, cognitive, and organizational factors
2. Measurement and research methods
3. Systems approach and HFE design
4. Digital human modeling and simulation
5. Various applications
This course is relevant for the student as it provides a deeper insight in the complexities of humans and the challenges of
considering human factors during the (re)design of products/services/systems in key application domains.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
1. Explain the value of the HFE discipline for design of products, services, and systems. (deepening LO2.6.1)
2. Explain the human physical, perceptual, cognitive, and organizational complexities in the context of socio-technical systems.
(deepening LO2.6.1)
3. Explain and apply HFE research methods to analyze HFE challenges at different levels (component, system, organization).
(deepening LO 1.1.2, 4.2.2)
4. Apply a systems approach in the design process to balance safety, performance, and satisfaction. (deepening LO3.2.1)
5. Apply computer models in HFE simulation
6. Critically analyze the context, present, and justify, with scientific rigor, the application of HFE solutions in mobility,
healthcare, sport or consumer product design deepening LO 5.1.1, 6.3.2.

description:
In this elective, students will develop a deeper knowledge of human behavior, motivation and experience. A focus will be on
understanding how to influence individuals, social and environmental factors as well as tools and strategies to design with.
During the course, we will apply the principles of psychology and behavior change on the themes of health, mobility and
sustainability. The content of this course is relevant for students, because it will help students to get a better understanding of
how design can support people to change their behavior.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
1. Explain which factors influence motivation and behavior using frameworks from psychological theories covered in the course
(deepening LO2.6.3).
2. Analyze existing behavior change interventions using motivation and behavior frameworks covered in the course.
3. Apply principles of motivation and behavior in their designs to measure, change and evaluate motivation and behavior
(deepening LO2.6.3).
4. Apply principles of human experience, emotion and perception in their design. (deepening LO2.6.2)
5. Evaluate design interventions and relate these results to theoretical frameworks that are discussed in the course.
6. Substantiate clearly their insights and design decisions during a presentation and in a written report (depeening LO 6.3.2)

description:
In this course students will learn how to study cultural and societal processes. The social and cultural perspective will empower
students to move beyond the individual as the unit of design. Through close readings of text and design case studies, we will
focus on the relationships between people, and between people and their environment.
The intention of most contemporary designers is to contribute to changes for better futures. This course critically reflects on this
concept of change. We will raise and address the questions about what exactly should be changed and what not, for whom these
changes are designed, how change happens over time and place, and what the possible roles of the designer in relation to change
might be. Insights from this course will inspire the development of students design visions and help them communicate the
outcomes of their socio-cultural analysis.
The content of this course is relevant for students, because what we design shapes cultures and societies and vice versa: their
logics and values influence our designs.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able:
1. to analyse the anthropological, sociological, political, and economic context that stage and shapes society. (2.8.1/2.8.2)
2. to identify social and cultural issues in design. (3.4.1)
3. to critically reflect on cultural and societal issues. (5.1.1; 5.4.2)
4. to communicate their analysis on culture and society. (6.3.1)

description:
The course offers an in depth program of learning profound communication and visualization skills, built on two parallel tiers:
(I) generative (including theoretic background) communication/ visualisation skills, and (II) explanatory communication/
visualisation skills. Each student is allowed to adapt his or her program by choosing a specific type of output format as part of
tier II: a chosen explanatory communication medium and related skill to learn
A fundament of visual literacy (included in this course) will support students in visualizing/ communicating elements of a design
situation or process. This visual literacy is needed to be able to unravel and manage information and perception thereof, to
visualize concepts, to capture and perhaps simplify a complex situation by communicating it visually. Both tier I and II concern
theoretic fundaments and realistic design situations.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
1. see, understand (and be able to explain) and accurately apply principles of visual composition (2d and 3d position, orientation,
character) to the visualized object/subject (deepening LO 1.1.2, 1.4.3, 1.5.1).
2. effectively consider, justify and apply principles of colour, saturation, brightness, chiaroscuro, when visualizing objects or
scenes.
3. accurately and effectively apply generative techniques and methodologies to externalize, reflect and communicate thoughts
and concepts (deepening LO 1.3, 1.4, 1.5).
4. apply vigour and signature in their lines, strokes, techniques, to design concepting (deepening LO 1.4.3, 6.3).
5. manually visualize a story: journey, process, narrative, storyboard, using story elements (frames, connections direction,
emphasis), focussing on clarity, communicativeness, accuracy (deepening LO 1.3.2, 1.4.2).
6. suitably and effectively utilize/apply specific explanatory visualization techniques: output media (deepening LO 6.3).

description:
Leadership and Project Organisation is a course meant for design students. In this elective, students will develop skills required
to organise and lead design projects. Students will learn about the aspects of different organisational settings, about leadership
styles applicable in a design context, about teamwork and about communication levels. Then, in a series of weekly cases,
students will make a project plan and will setup and maintain collaborations within the team and with multiple stakeholders. The
relevance of this course for students is that they acquire skills that empower them to realise their goals as a lead designer or
project leader in various organisational settings.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
LO1. to distinguish between various leadership styles and organisational settings and to select leadership styles that fit design
and innovation environments (deepening LO 6.2.2.).
LO2. to distinguish between communication levels and to select and apply levels according to the situation (deepening LO
6.3.1).
LO3. to select and apply techniques to effectively plan and organise design projects and to manage progress of design projects
(deepening LO 1.1.3 ).
LO4. to demonstrate collaborating effectively with teams and stakeholders in design and innovation processes in different
organisational and cultural settings (deepening LO 6.1).

description:
In this course the student will collaborate with experienced researchers of our faculty on mastering scientific research in design
and beyond. The student will discuss published research projects with them, and walk in their shoes during an academic research
project
Mastering research methods will help the student to develop scientific inquiry skills that are crucial for a plethora of if not all -
courses at a university. In any (design) project, it is useful to be able to assess existing knowledge, and decide on the need for
gathering new knowledge through research. Moreover, input for solid argumentation typically comes from existing or new
research. Knowledge of strengths and shortcomings of research methods is key to stand ones ground.
The course offers hands on research experience beyond creating merely awareness. With the help of experienced researchers,
this course provides armor against scientifically proven claims, triggers curiosity into the unknown, and shows the merits of
scientific research.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
1. evaluate research in terms of theoretical and practical implications, limitations, and generalizability (deepening LO 4.1.1, LO
4.3.1)
2. set-up research to conduct an empirical study for answering a research question that matches the topic and practical
considerations laid out by the supervisor, and analyze the research accordingly (deepening LO 4.2.1, LO4.2.2, LO4.2.3)
3. present and report research and its outcomes adequately (deepening LO 4.3.2)

description:
In this elective, students will experience that materials are not only items in a data base that need to be selected, but that they can
also mix and combine e.g. bio-based and degradable components to create their own materials. Why not using a starch-based
material to make an edible lunch box, or designing your own bio-based cover for your tablet; why not using maizena-sand
mixture to make a flower pot or a mussel shell composite to 3D-print a ceramic lamp? The use of bio-based materials is at the
core of this elective.
Students will learn appropriate tools which are needed to design with such new (and often not yet existing) material composites.
How can you best model, make and test a product made by a new material designed by yourself? Manufacturing, testing and user
aspects of the case studies will be topics in this elective.
The content of this course is relevant for students, because they will gain knowledge and insight on how selection of appropriate
manufacturing techniques and of materials will condition the design of a product. The performance (technical and experiential)
of finished products is ultimately determined by underlying materials and manufacturing characteristics.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
1. Categorise the materials based on understanding their common properties and characteristics as well as variety of
manufacturing technologies and the related opportunities and limitations for embodiment design (deepening LO2.2.2).
2. Measure and evaluate the basic mechanical properties of materials with e.g. tensile test, bending test and hardness. In addition,
they will become familiar with experiential characterization of their materials used in their case studies (deepening LO 2.2.2).
3. Describe and analyse both design possibilities and technological limitations for their selected manufacturing technologies in
their embodiment design, including the peculiarities of bio-based materials (deepening LO 2.2.2).
4. Use and analyse modelling (SolidWorks+ Finite Element Analysis) of more complex shaped products and calculate the loaded
product and production aspects such as feasibility (deepening LO 2.1.2).
5. Recommend a suitable material and manufacturing method in a given design situation, taking into consideration a given set of
boundary conditions and sustainability aspects (deepening LO 3.3.2).

description:
Mechatronics course offers unique opportunities for students to design smart, affordable, reliable and versatile consumer
products. For this, students will learn knowledge and skills related to electronics, digital signal processing, control, (data-driven)
modelling, simulation, prototyping, as well as mechatronic design principles, where the key is to achieve synergy between
mechanical and electronic components while striving for added value, e.g. economical and user benefit, in consumer products.
Based on prior knowledge on dynamics, electronics and software, and envisioning the future of smart product design, the
mechatronic course will further explore the design of mechatronics products by focusing on three key questions:
1. What are the working principles of mechatronic system and how can (micro) electronics be applied in the system?
2. How can Mechatronic design principles be applied in designing mechatronic products and how do these principles affect the
product?
3. How can we implement and optimize the performance of mechatronic system by combining the knowledge on physical
models and electronics using intelligently balanced control strategies?

This technology elective will provide students with the knowledge required to understand, design, and evaluate machine learning
systems in the context of the design of intelligent products, services, and systems (iPSSs). Machine learning (ML) is a
computational approach that aims at giving computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed (A. Samuel,
1959). Smart thermostats, voice-based personal assistants, autonomous vehicles, traffic control systems, online social networks,
web shopping platforms, content creation platforms, personal health appliances: much of current and future iPSSs are powered
by ML technology, influencing and shaping our interests, habits, lives, and society. To meaningfully envision and design future
iPSSs that is beneficial and useful to people and society, designers must: engage with the details of how ML systems see the
world, reason about it, and interact with it; experience the quirks, biases, and failures of ML technology; contend with how
agency, initiative, trust, and explainability mediate the interaction between human and iPSSs; and understand how functionalities
enabled by ML can be designed in iPSSs. Students in this course will gain practical experience with ML technology and learn
how to think critically of what ML systems can do, and how they could and should be integrated into iPSSs.
The course will cover the following topics:
1. AI and ML in intelligent products, services, and systems (design). The students will be introduced to the role that Artificial
Intelligence and, more specifically, Machine Learning technology play in iPSSs, in their design process, and in their lifecycle.
The most important ML concepts, terminology, paradigms, and methods will also be described and exemplified.
2. Text Processing methods for iPSSs. Building on the knowledge acquired in the DATA course, students will be introduced to
existing ML techniques for text processing (parsing, analysis, generation), and will practice with their use in realistic design
contexts.
3. Image Processing methods for iPSSs. Students will be introduced to existing ML techniques for image processing (acquisition,
analysis, generation), and will practice with their use in realistic design contexts.
4. Creating Machine Learning Models Students. will deepen their knowledge in how machine learning models could be trained,
and on how their performance could be evaluated. Specific attention will be devoted to the task of training data a) design, b)
creation, and c) usage in realistic adoption scenarios.
5. Designing iPSSs that include Machine Learning technology. In this final module, students will learn how to design (using
human-centred approaches) intelligent products, services, and systems. Students will understand which issues could impact the
experience of people when interacting with iPSSs, and learn to assess how ML technology can and should be integrated into
iPSSs.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
- LO1: explain common terminology used when discussing about Machine Learning algorithms, systems and their evaluation
(deepening LO 2.4.4)
- LO2: identify the requirements for a Machine Learning system (deepening LO 2.5.2)
- LO3: describe and compare different classes of Machine Learning techniques (deepening LO2.4.1, LO 2.4.4, LO 3.2.3)
- LO4: describe and compare design decisions in the context of iPSSs design and defend the relevance and correctness of their
choices (deepening LO2.5.1, LO 5.1.1)
- LO5: recommend appropriate Machine Learning technique(s) for a certain problem domain (deepening LO1.2.2, LO1.2.3,
LO3.4.3, LO 5.2.2)
- LO6: assess their team members' work with respect to methodological soundness and contribution. (deepening LO1.5.4, LO
1.6.1, LO 5.1.2)

description:
In the Bachelor Final Project (BFP) students apply the knowledge and skills they have gathered and competences they have been
working on so far in the bachelor. In this way the project can be seen as a ´Proof of Competence´ for the whole Bachelor
programme. At the same time the project is part of the learning trajectory to become a BSc Industrial Design Engineer and
therefore the directional activities are corresponding with the Final Attainment Levels.
BFP (Dutch: Bachelor Eind Project (BEP)) revolves around a design assignment for a real client, with the exploration and
application of (new) knowledge in context. This project requires students to learn:
individual cooperation with a client,
to plan and anticipate,
to be sensitive to their own project and performance, and
to be willing and able to correct the project if required.
Effectively, this means a student needs to (learn to) individually manage the relation between cause (effort) and effect (results)
and act responsible. Participants in BEP will be offered specific workshops as support for their design process and presentation.
Once started, each student develops their own design goal and project goals within the given case, using the Navigation Canvas
(Van Erp et al 2020). The student also sets up a project structure and planning accordingly, including:
strategies for integrating knowledge,
application of design tools and methods, and
fruitful cooperation.
Students can use the Navigation Canvas (Van Erp et al 2020) to encounter any typical phase of the product development process
in BEP:
the fuzzy front end (strategy building),
ideation and concepting, embodiment and
the fuzzy back-end (implementation plan).
Depending on the given case and the goals of each individual student, focus and emphasis can lay on different phases and
elements. The set up for the project and its deliverables are agreed upon by the design coach and the client. Based on the shifting
field of work, the methodology of the course will be based on classic methodology via Design Thinking to Systemic Design
Thinking.
Three times during the project the achieved results and plans are presented to and discussed with the client. At the end each
student should deliver a credible design proposal that offers value for all relevant stakeholders.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
1. Navigating
Students are able to apply appropriate process models, methods and tools to navigate an iterative design process (1.1).
2. Integrating
Students are able to integrate the interests of different stakeholders to generate designs that have sustainable impact on
environment, society and economy (1.2).
3. Framing
Students are able to explore complex problem situations and use the insights to frame (open) design challenges (1.3).
4. Concepting
Students are able to explore the design space and generate innovative concepts (1.4).
5. Visualising & Prototyping
Students are able to make concepts tangible through visualizing, modelling and prototyping to develop, communicate and
evaluate designs (1.5).
6. Evaluating
Students are able to evaluate design outcomes with regards to feasibility, desirability and viability as well as the sustainable
impact on the environment, society and economy (1.6).
7. Professional Development
a. Students are able to explain the global field of design and to position themselves in this field (5.3).
b. Students are able to set up a plan to develop themselves towards a preferred learning and working career with a high degree of
autonomy (5.4).
8. Collaboration & Communication
a. Students are able to initiate and maintain various collaborations effectively to fulfil a specific purpose within the design
process (6.1).
b. Students are able to present and report research and design outcomes using a variety of media (6.3).

description:
Design will play a key role in the transition to a circular economy (CE). Most of todays products are designed with little regard
for what happens when we no longer want them. Consequently, products are wasted, in terms of both materials and value. And
waste is design gone wrong!
In a circular economy, products loop back into the production system through repair, refurbishment, remanufacturing and
eventually, recycling. By doing this, we extend their useful life, capture value and design out waste.
This course will strengthen the design skills of bachelor students to tackle the transition from our linear 'take-make-waste'
economy to a circular economy. This elective course provides students theory as well as practicum assignments, addressing the
business and design aspects of going circular. The student will learn about and develop circular business models and recovery
strategies applied to a specific design challenge.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
1. Describe the basic principles and terms underlying the circular economy (deepening LO 3.2).
2. Explain business models and recovery strategies that can deliver value in the circular economy (deepening LO 2.10.2 + 3.2).
3. Evaluate the circularity and sustainability of a product (deepening LO 1.6.4).
4. Apply CE principles to redesign a (linear) product, addressing both the business case and recovery strategies (deepening LO
2.10.2, 3.2, 3.3.1, 3.3.2).
5. Provide relevant arguments for your design decisions, using the theory, methods and tools offered (deepening LO 5.2.2).

description:
Bij Ontwerpdidactiek kunnen studenten de basisbeginselen leren van didactiek en hun kennis van het ontwerpproces en
ontwerpmethoden verdiepen.
Ze ontdekken hoe ze hun inzichten het beste aan medestudenten (IO) kunnen overbrengen.
Het keuzevak Ontwerpdidactiek bevat onder andere de volgende onderdelen:
(cid:9)Didactiek: theorie over het coachen van het ontwerpproces van medestudenten;
(cid:9)Stage lopen bij DP2, waarbij de student ervaart, voelt, ontdekt, experimenteert met wat er bij de theorie is behandeld;
(cid:9)Verdieping van de theorie m.b.t. ontwerpen, ontwerptechnieken en ontwerpmethoden.
Door het evalueren van video-opnamen van hun eigen workshop en tijdens begeleidingsgesprekken kunnen studenten hun
vaardigheden op deze onderdelen verder aanscherpen.
Parallel hieraan komen ze elke week terug in een intervisiebijeenkomst waarin met medestudenten wordt besproken wat ze in de
praktijk hebben geleerd.
Studenten die dit vak met goed resultaat afronden kunnen in aanmerking komen om studentassistent te worden bij IO-vakken.

Reimagining Mobility is an elective design course that teaches the 3rd year IDE undergraduates how to envision meaningful
mobility solutions in different levels of innovationproduct, service, or societal-system levelsthat harmonize people and different
transportation modalities.
The content of this course is relevant for students who are interested in mobility theme, because through an iterative design
process, they will be equipped with the domain knowledge on general mobility sector (in product/ service/societal-system
levels), an ability to apply the previously acquired design mindset and skill sets (from other design courses in the faculty) to
analyze real-world problems in the mobility sector, and an ability to design new mobility concepts for people in transit and
stakeholders in the mobility ecosystem.
The course will be instrumental for the projects that students will execute in master courses and for determining the role they
wish to play as design professionals in mobility related societal challenges.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
(cid:9)LO1. Analyze transportation modalities of present context (e.g., autonomous driving, busses, trams, trains, aviation, airport to
micro-mobility, etc.)
(cid:9)LO2. Create a meaningful mobility solution built upon emerging technologies, making use of the design mindset and skill sets
acquainted throughout the previous years
(cid:9)LO3. Explain the novel ways by arguing how the future mobility solutions newly interact with stakeholders in the mobility
ecosystem
(cid:9)LO4. Describe design knowledge across the iterative design innovation process and explain their design journey.

description:
Health is an elective course where the students will gain knowledge on designing products, services and interventions in the
context of health with its specific stakeholders and conditions. The course will provide an overview of relevant topics,
developments and challenges in health, such as advanced health technologies, patient experience, digitalization, regulations, etc.
The Dutch health care landscape will be explored by capita selecta lectures and workshops. The lectures and workshops will
offer the students different perspectives in the complex health system and will be provided by different stakeholders active in the
domain of health, such as patients, informal care givers, healthcare professionals, designers, researcher, industry, etc. This
course will also present a sneak preview of the topics, projects and research themes of the Medisign specialization. Medisign is a
master specialization at the Faculty of Industrial Design Engineering and aims to educate dedicated and skilled industrial design
engineers in the field of healthcare.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing the course students are able to:
1.(cid:9)Illustrate the complexity of the health system and its stakeholders by mapping a patient journey (deepening LO 3.2.1)
2.(cid:9)Understand the different perspectives of the stakeholders and reflect on their own perspectives (deepening LO 5.1.1)
3.(cid:9)Reflect and motivate their own role as a designer in the field of healthcare (deepening LO 5.3.2)

description:
The applied goal of this course is to support students in creating a meaningful portfolio that will allow them to present
themselves as designers, for example to future coaches, potential companies for internship, graduation projects, possible jobs and
so on.
To achieve this goal, students will explore their identity as a designer. First, by reflecting on the design experiences they had so
far (and collected in the IDME activities. Next, by exploring what motivates them, what inspires them, what values and future
vision they have, what their position in the Design Field could be, and so on.
In addition, students will explore different means of visual and verbal presentation, to discover which modes of expression fit
their Identity. This will allow them to align content and form of the portfolio.
The coherence of the portfolio will be ensured by emphasizing during the course on the art of storytelling.
The course will not conclude with a finished portfolio as a means in itself, but with the foundation for creating professional
portfolios in the future.
The second goal of this course is to introduce the students to the more theoretical aspects of the different perspectives on the
concept of Identity. Students will explore these concepts while creating their own.
This theoretical foundation will be valuable for students, first, to have a solid basis for their portfolio, and next, in their future
design work, where designing for others always implicates awareness of identity, and the dilemmas this concept elicits.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
1. Present themselves, their design work and their future aspirations in an effective, inspiring and convincing way, using the art
of storytelling (deepening LO 5.4.3).
2. Position themselves in the field of Design (deepening LO 5.3.2).
3. Understand the relation between content, form and goal of a presentation about themselves (deepening LO 6.3.1).
4. Distinguish between the different aspects and theories on Identity
5. Construct a personal concept of Identity that supports them in their personal presentations

description:
Dit vak wordt in het NL gegeven, maar alle literatuur zal in het Engels zijn.
This course focuses on the organizational and behavioral context of the innovative design process, its relationship to startups, to
socio-technical systems and to entrepreneurial behavior.
At IDE we train designers to develop new and innovative products/services/systems from initiation to validated concept, and no
further, so no implementation! The course will extend this 'limited' focus in two ways: first, to encompass the trajectory from
concept to realization; secondly, to include the perspective of innovation actors other than the designers themselves
(stakeholders).
In the course you will learn that the organizational actors from different disciplines should be seen as the first users of the
concept delivered by them/designers. The course will focus on these so-called 'intermediate users' who sit between the design
concept and the end user, which is your traditional focus. You will learn to assess the organizational and behavioral context of
the intermediate users with a view to designing (innovative) concepts that are ready for implementation. In addition, you will
learn that the implementation of outside-the-box concepts requires entrepreneurial behavior on the part of most organizational
actors to come to fruition.
To ensure that the concepts from theory become relevant, this course has been set up as a Mixed-Classroom course in which
students work together with an innovation professional from the field. From week 5, each student team has its own customer
with an organizational innovation challenge. As a team, you will be asked to assess the organizational context, understand the
challenge and provide a workable response. Most customers will speak Dutch.
Finally, you will also reflect on their individual personality traits from the perspective of the entrepreneurial journey from
concept to realization.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course, students are able to:
1.(cid:9)Apply theoretical framework of implementation/scaling processes to design concepts for the purpose of realization planning
(deepening LO 1.1.3)
2.(cid:9)Assess and appraise organizational processes with the purpose of mapping absorptive and innovative capacities in relation to
concepts
3.(cid:9)Explicate and contrast the theoretical principles of designing, engineering, innovating and entrepreneuring
4.(cid:9)Describe differences and similarities between new-venture and corporate entrepreneurship
5.(cid:9)Know how to apply the notions of frontloading, disciplinas and intermediate users to the case study
6.(cid:9)Apply their understanding of technology development from the perspective of socio-technical systems to the situation of
concept design
7.(cid:9)Explain theory by a lecture to inform an audience of lay people (deepening LO 6.3.2)
8.(cid:9)Show awareness of personality traits and apply self-knowledge for envisioning their role within entrepreneurial innovation
processes (based on personality tests) (deepening LO 6.2.2).

description:
This course allows students to experience the day-to-day reality of engineering design; team work, deal with competition, scarce
recourses and limited time. During this course students (in groups of max. 5) will design and build a robot that has to perform
what seems to be a simple task. Every group will start from an identical toolkit containing electric motors, gearboxes and a
variety of mechanical parts. An exciting competition on Saturday April 1 (no joke) will determine who can solve the task best
while dealing with the competition at the same time. And like in the real world, anything could happen during the runtime of the
course.
Learning objectives of this course include team work, adaptation skills, practical electronics and prototyping during a design-
build-test cycle. During the course, students will build upon team working skills, by reviewing their team performance using the
7C model (Janssen, 1999). The two deliverables of the course are a report on the robots performance and an individual journal in
which students reflect on their role as a team member.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
- Design and build a robot that can perform a simple task (deepening LO 1.6.1, LO 2.5.1, LO 2.5.2)
- Contribute to team work effectively and reflect on their contribution to the teams performance (deepening LO 5.1.2, LO 5.1.3,
LO 6.2.1 & LO 6.2.3).
- Analyze and estimate the success rate of their own robot versus the competitors robot and act upon this (deepening LO 1.5.3,
LO 1.6.1 & LO 1.6.2)

description:
In this elective, students will learn to conduct simple biomechanical analyses of human-product interaction. Furthermore, they
will learn about how to model, analyze, and evaluate musculoskeletal system of human beings during daily activities and product
use. It gives an introduction in the different structures in the body (like bones, ligaments, and tendons), their mechanical
properties, and the mechanical load in order to develop design requirements.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course students are able to:
1. Apply basic anatomy, mathematics and physics in the context of biomechanics in product use.
2. Systematically model, analyze, and evaluate the biomechanical behavior in simple static and dynamic situations (deepening
LO 2.1.2).
3. Apply biomechanical principles aligned with the human body (including bodily functioning and psychophysics) to create
design requirements (deepening LO 2.6.1).

description:
In this technological and methodological elective, students will gather tools and acquire knowledge to critically evaluate
(interactive and intelligent) technological prototypes and set the stage for the next iteration of the design phase by eliciting
actionable design guidelines based on comprehensive empirical analysis. The technological component of this course is
demonstrated by the strong focus on the improvement of IPSS (intelligent products, services, and systems) such as,
conversational assistants, wearables, etc.
Instead of examining the complete design cycle, students will focus solely on the quantitative assessment of IPSS and examine
their cognitive, perceptual, and experiential effects. To this end, students will learn and add skills to their methodological toolkit,
which will enable them to a) design sound experiments (with Control and Experimental groups), b) use sensing technologies
(e.g., eye-tracking) and adapt existing data-acquisition tools (e.g., NASA TLX, MSLQ), c) identify the right statistical tests
(descriptive vs. inferential; comparison vs. regression), d) discriminate correlation from causation and identify confounding
factors, and e) understand the proper means of communicating their quantitative analysis and results.
The content of this course is relevant for students because they learn how to systematically assess their designs with standardized
practices and communicate their findings with multiple stakeholders and a broader design-research community. In this way, this
course offers an essential ingredient in students transformation from a UX Designer to a UX Researcher.
In this course, the student will become familiar with the 5-stage Design Analytics Process (DAP) i.e., design diagnostics, study
design synthesis, experimentation, data analysis, and design prescription.
learning_objectives:
Upon finishing this course, students are able to:
1: Describe the design unknowns or flaws of a given product, service, or system (deepening LO 1.3.3, LO 1.6.3).
2: Formulate research questions and pertinent hypotheses to empirically evaluate the given technology (deepening LO 4.2.1).
3: Design an experiment protocol to validate the research hypotheses (deepening LO 4.2.2, LO 1.6.1).
