description:
Model Predictive Control (MPC) is perhaps the most effective optimal control strategy for constrained dynamical systems. The
basic concept of MPC is to exploit a dynamic model to forecast the system behavior, and optimize the forecast to determine the
control input as the best decision at the current time. With emphasis on constrained linear systems, the course will present the
theoretical fundamentals of MPC, such as Lyapunov stability, optimality and robustness, and its computational methods, such as
quadratic programming.
learning_objectives:
- Derive state prediction matrices from discrete-time linear models
- Design the cost function, state and input constraints
- Design MPC controllers with guaranteed recursive feasibility and asymptotic stability via appropriate terminal cost and
constraint set
- Formulate and solve constrained-linear-quadratic MPC problems via quadratic programming
- Implement and simulate closed-loop systems controlled by MPC on Matlab
- Design MPC controllers with integral action for reference tracking

description:
(cid:9)Modelling. The course will cover the basics of Lagrangian modelling, I.e. employing energy balances and the Euler-Lagrange
equations to arrive to closed form state-space dynamical equations for system analysis and control design. Bond-graph modelling
will be covered as a powerful tool for modelling engineering systems, especially when different physical domains are involved.
The basic ideas of model reduction, a technique to reduce the complexity of dynamical models, is also covered in the course. The
fundamental differences and connections between continuous vs discrete time modelling will be discussed. Similarly, frequency
domain modelling is also discussed with practical motivations for frequency vs time domain modelling.
(cid:9)Finite State Models. A brief introduction to models traditionally employed for computation, e.g. finite state machines, automata,
and petri-nets, will be provided. Particular attention will be given to the applicability of these models to provide high-level
dynamic descriptions of discrete-event systems and for behaviour specifications of designs.
(cid:9)Hybrid systems. The course will finalize with a short introduction to hybrid systems through the formalisms of: Hybrid automata
and jump-flow systems, and presenting a brief number of interesting subclasses of hybrid systems, e.g. PWA systems, and timed
-automata.

The purpose of the course is to introduce the students to basic concepts and results in physical modeling and the theory of

description:
The course introduces design thinking in socio-technical systems as the core orientation of the entire SEPAM master. Students
learn about designing complex technological systems in multi-actor environments. It starts from understanding socio-technical
systems towards creating artefacts to realize change in socio-technical systems. Different perspectives on systems design are
discussed to provide students with a background for working with designers from different disciplines. Thereby, the course lays
the foundation for further design-oriented courses. Typical questions the module addresses are:
- How to explore a problem situation?
- How to oversee a design challenge?
- How to formulate a design task?
- What is a suitable design approach for specific design challenges?
Students follow lectures and work together in groups on a specific challenge to put the knowledge into practice: learning by
doing.
learning_objectives:
After completion of the course, the student is able to
- use and differentiate discuss concepts and terminology related to the design in socio-technical systems
- analyze a problem situation in complex, technological, large-scale systems in multi-actor environments
- use and combine methods and tools for requirements analysis and conceptual design
- use and compare methods and tools that facilitate systems design and engineering
- apply and compare methods and tools related to decision, project and risk management
- determine a suitable design approach for specific socio-technical design challenges
- use and combine methods and tools for systems analysis and modelling to address complexity and uncertainty in design
processes

description:
Previous courses have focused on, first, diagnosing the complexity of systems and problems and, then, designing for systems and
their institutions in the midst of this complexity. This course on multi-actor decision-making goes one step further: (reflecting
on) realizing change.
We focus on the actors in the system. How do they behave, individually and collectively? What does the system look like from
an actor perspective? Why does intentional change often appear so hard? What limits the designability of systems?
By studying characteristics of complex engineering systems (e.g. the increased importance of IT for design, the increased
interdependencies between systems) as well as the specific actor characteristics (e.g. the global character of the manufacturers
and supply chains, issues of plurality and inclusiveness we identify key factors that affect intentional change (i.e. the wickedness
of problems, public values, strategic behaviour of actors and dynamics of the system). How do these factors affect decision-
making and design and change of complex engineering systems?
How can we assess the consequences of this decision-making complexity and how does this affect the potential for interventions
for (re)design in these systems in deliberate and responsible ways?
In this course, we identify key characteristics which affect multi-actor decision making in complex engineering designs.
Furthermore, we assess how and under which conditions process managerial tactics may help to manage multi-actor decision-
making with its plural rationalities and dynamics of negotiation and design.
learning_objectives:
At the end of this course, students will be able to
explain why actors in networks behave as they do, and how their behaviour evolves
describe different network structures and their practical implications
assess the designability of institutions, systems, policies and technologies
argue why certain process managerial tactics might work under which conditions
create case-specific process managerial tactics to anticipate complex decision-making.
assess the quality of process designs
reflect on multi-actor decision-making in light of broader scientific and public policy trends and debates

description:
Suppose we want to switch to a hydrogen based economy in which fuel cell cars are used as power plants. Or suppose we want a
fully automated inland terminal. And what about the construction of multifunctional dikes? You cannot just realize that but you
have to be aware of the relevant legal and institutional framework. That framework will enable you to make things happen, but it
can also contain constraints.
This course focuses on the legal and institutional framework to take into account with that kind of projects. Are there for instance
legal instruments to force people to switch to fuel cell cars? And to what institutional layer do those instruments belong? Are
they easy to change? Or: can the government subsidize the transition to a fully automated inland terminal? What are the
constraints? And can we work around those constraints? Or: what exactly has to be studied for the environmental impact
learning_objectives:
At the end of the course, students are able to:
- Relate legal instruments to the institutional framework
- Work with the law as a system
- Relate the legal instruments to the institutional framework
- Identify the legal borders of the design space regarding a socio technical system
- Identify relevant law for a socio technical system
- Apply relevant law to a socio technical system and identify barriers and opportunities
- Deal with legal language

description:
Our human society consists of many intertwined Large Scale Socio-Technical Systems (LSSTS), such as infrastructures,
industrial networks, the financial and legal systems etc. Environmental pressures created by these systems on Earth's carrying
capacity are leading to exhaustion of natural resources, loss of habitats and biodiversity, and are causing a resource and climate
crisis. To avoid this sustainability crisis, we urgently need to transform our production and consumption patterns. Given that we,
as inhabitants of this planet, are part of a complex and integrated global system where and how should we begin this
transformation? And how can we also ensure that our transformation efforts will lead to a sustainable world?
Society, with its industrial, social, economic en institutional systems, embedded in the planetary ecosystems are Complex
Adaptive Systems (CAS). According to John Holland CAS are "...a dynamic network of many agents (which may represent
cells, species, individuals, firms, nations) acting in parallel, constantly acting and reacting to what the other agents are doing. The
control of a CAS tends to be highly dispersed and decentralized. If there is to be any coherent behavior in the system, it will have
to to arise from competition and cooperation among the agents themselves. The overall behavior of the system is the result of a
huge number of decisions made every moment" by many individual agents.
Understanding Complex Adaptive Systems requires tools that themselves are complex to create and understand. Shalizi defines
Agent Based Modeling as "An agent is a persistent thing which has some state we find worth representing, and which interacts
with other agents, mutually modifying each others states. The components of an agent-based model are a collection of agents and
their states, the rules governing the interactions of the agents and the environment within which they live."
This course has two focus points: 1-Complex Adaptive Systems Theory and 2- Agent Based Modelling.
We will explore Complex Adaptive Systems theory, across many different types of systems. Lectures will be quite philosophical
in nature, and are meant to provide a coherent, high level understanding of systems, their properties and their interactions.
Lecture materials provide further reading to broaden your view and deepen your understanding.
Second focus point is developing Agent Based Modelling skills. This course is not meant as an introduction to basic
programming, or a thorough introduction to NetLogo environment, but will rather focus on understand the concepts of ABM
and how model design choices affect the model created and how it can be used. Additional reading materials are provided for
self-study in getting up to speed on basic programming and NetLogo.
learning_objectives:
The two goal of the course are, first, to understand Complex Adaptive Systems theory and its relation to the socio-technical
systems around us. Second goal is for the student to learn about the the basics of Agent Based Modeling.
More formally, there are 5 course goals:
1. Students should know the definitions of CAS properties, as listed in the course topics
2. Students should be able to identify relevant properties of a system and determine whether or not the system can be classified
as CAS.
3. Students should be able to create a coherent description of a system from both top down and bottom up
4. Students should be able to understand, modify and create Agent Based Simulations in NetLogo.
5. Students should be able to reflect on the traditional engineering systems thinking from the CAS perspective and understand
the implications of changing the traditional perspective.

description:
If one wants to design effective (transport) systems, one needs to understand the behavior of -future- users of these systems, e.g.
the market share of a new public transport service. If one wants to design effective (transport) policies, one needs to know how
people will respond to these policies, e.g. impact of a tax incentive on electric vehicle sales. This course sets out to provide
students with in-depth knowledge and hands-on experience with behavioral theories, mathematical models and statistical
methods that have proved very effective in understanding and predicting human choice behaviour.
Importantly, this course takes a quantitative (i.e., mathematical and statistical) perspective on choice behaviour; this is quite
different from the usual perspective in behavioral science-courses, which tends to be more qualitative. More specifically, we
formalize behavioral theories into mathematical models, which we then estimate on empirical datasets using cutting edge
statistical methods. In combination, the estimated econometric 'choice models' support rigorous analysis and forecasts of
quantitative phenomena, thereby playing a crucial role in private and public sector policy development.
The theories, models and methods that are taught in this course are applicable -and have been used- throughout a wide variety of
domains, including but not limited to Transportation, Health, Marketing, Environment & Energy, and Political sciences. As such,
our course optimally prepares students for a wide range of (quantitative, empirical) topics for their graduation projects.
The course will cover both canonical (and Nobel Prize winning) methods which are based on the notion of rational decision
making, as well as more recently proposed ones which are based on notions of bounded rationality (economic psychology) and
moral decision-making. Both lecturers are highly active in the international research community, and their work forms part of the
academic state of the art.
learning_objectives:
Students will acquire an in-depth knowledge concerning the below mentioned theories, models and methods, as well as the skills
to use them in their own research. Finally, they will acquire an understanding of the usefulness and limitations of these theories,
models and methods; and an understanding of how they can and should be used in combination.
Knowledge transfer will take the form of a series of lectures, whereas skills will be (further) developed in tailor made computer
exercises. Specifically, during the computer exercises, students will learn how to design a statistically optimal choice
experiment, and how to analyze data obtained from such experiments. In addition, they will learn how to interpret the outcomes
of such analyses and how to use them to evaluate and design policies.
- Choice behaviour modelling methods (van Cranenburgh)
o Discrete choice theory and the Logit model
o Advanced (Mixed) Logit models
o Choice models for bounded rationality and morality
- Stated Choice data collection methods (Molin)
o Data-collection paradigms
o Stated choice experiments
o Efficient design approaches.

description:
Students are challenged to tackle an integrated energy system design problem in the form of a modelling project. Students are
expected to come up with a creative (set of) design(s). Afterwards, they evaluate the expected performance of one or more of
these designs as a future system or improvement to existing energy systems.
The design challenge is complex and can only be met: 1) by taking into account dynamics on the short and long term, 2) by
tapping into relevant knowledge on technological developments, 3) by using various quantitative analyses, 4) by considering
various parts of the value chain, in terms of energy, mass, financial and information flows and 6) by relating and addressing the
multi-actor and multi-level complexities.
The quantitative analyses are to be executed with a set of quantitative tools, some used in earlier courses in the Energy Track,
some developed by research institutes and companies, and others used in ongoing academic research at the faculty, made
available for this course.
learning_objectives:
(cid:9)Understand and execute the main steps in the design of integrated energy systems
(cid:9)Is able to provide an overview of and explore the design space of integrated energy systems, consisting of multiple carriers,
multiple relevant levels, multiple time-scales, multiple sectors
(cid:9)Is able to identify and conceptualize core processes that affect the performance of an integrated energy system that play out on
short, medium and long term
(cid:9)Is able to select, develop and use quantitative simulation models for designing integrated energy systems
(cid:9)Is able to reflect on aspects that are placed outside the design space, i.e. the relationship to food, water, built environment, etc.

description:
More and more data is available using various sources like databases, social media or the Internet of Things (IoT). Information
sharing requires the integration of these systems. The ability to execute and process data is a key capability required by public
and private organizations. The large variety of heterogeneous data, applications and business processes results in a complex and
fragmented landscape that need to be dealt with when architecting and engineering new systems. Path dependencies and legacy
block the easy integration, whereas at the same time new technologies appear that need to be integrated in the complex systems
landscape.
The purpose of this course is to teach the architectural design of innovative and large-scale ICT infrastructures and services in
the light of the challenges imposed by the requirements from the systems physical, economic and social environment. Emphasis
will be put on the concepts and role of ICT-architecture and modelling in order to properly design ICT solutions within a multi-
actor context. For this purpose application and data integration technologies and information and system quality theories will be
addressed.
learning_objectives:
-The student is familiar with the state-of-the-art knowledge of ICT-architecting, design and governance within the field of large-
scale ICT-systems within a multi-actor context
-The student is able to describe basic concepts related to architecting and designing large and complex ICT-infrastructures and
service systems within a multi-actor context.
-The student should master architecture theories, methods and tools with the ability to combine and switch between them when
dealing with complex ICT-problems.
-The student is able to structure and analyze problems and identify dilemmas arising during the design process with regard to
designing large ICT-systems within a multi-actor context.
-The student is able to apply system engineering and architecture-based approaches, methods and tools to deal with problems
with regard to designing large ICT-systems.
-The student is able to report about the use of architectural concepts, methods and tools for translating business needs into ICT-
designs within constellation of public and private actors.
faculty: Electrical Engineering, Mathematics and Computer Science

description:
Mobile apps, Internet-of-Things, cloud edge architectures and sensors are enabling a range of new I&C services. These services
are typically offered in ecosystems of interdependent actors. However, designing services that add value for users as well as
ecosystem stakeholders is challenging.
In this course, you learn how to design practical ICT services and develop a valorization plan. The course contains two main
learning_objectives:
After the course, you are able to:
- Analyze practical ICT services by applying concepts of design science research, action design research, agile development and
service engineering
- Evaluate practical requirements and make informed choices on supporting technologies and platforms, with specific attention to
autonomous driving, medical IoT, AI, XR, and edge computing technologies
- Evaluate an ICT-enabled service concept through semi-structured interviews
- Design and illustrate a value-adding service concept driven by ICT
- Design a valorization plan that explicitly covers how and when to involve external stakeholders in a design process and
integrate the ICT service with value network

course_name: Advanced Evaluation Methods for Transport Policy Decision-
description:
Transport policies are almost always controversial. Several methods are applied worldwide to support decision-making in
transport. Nowadays, societal cost-benefit analysis (CBA) and Multi Criteria Decision Methods (MCDM) are the most
prominent and well-known transport policy appraisal methods. In this course you will learn about the newest scientific
developments in these appraisal methods. Additionally, you will learn about new appraisal methods such as Participatory Value
Evaluation.
learning_objectives:
Describe and explain traditional evaluation methods (CBA and MCDM) and non-traditional evaluation methods.
Explain the pros and cons of different methods for different evaluation circumstances
Describe the ethical critiques for different types of evaluation methods
Define/pick a research gap (to be used in the paper)
Write an academic paper, based on completed case study exercise, where: A research gap that the student can fill/contribute to
is identified ; Pros and cons of ONE chosen method are critically reflected upon; The suitability of the method is convincingly
argued;
The results are analysed and interpreted, criticised with particular attention to ethical issues; Policy recommendations are made
on the use of the results

description:
In this course students learn how to perform travel behaviour research and how to translate the findings from such research into
recommendations for transport policy design.
The students will acquire knowledge about six modelling paradigms in travel behaviour research, namely the econometric,
psychological, geographical, biographical, marketing and sociological paradigm. The strengths and weaknesses of each paradigm
will be discussed. In addition, three state-of-the-art methods to analyse travel behaviour (structural equation models, latent class
choice models and latent class clusters models) will be treated. These methods figure prominently within the six modelling
paradigms. For each method there will be a group assignment (so 3 in total). These group assignments will count for 50% of the
grade.
learning_objectives:
After this course the students will be able:
(1)(cid:9)to carry out travel behavior research using three state-of-the-art statistical methods, namely structural equation modeling,
latent class cluster analysis and latent class choice models.
(2)(cid:9)to translate the study findings to recommendations for transport policy design.

description:
The transport system is continuously changing due to the introduction of many innovative concepts in vehicles, infrastructure,
and services, examples being the introduction of the car, e-bike or high speed train (vehicles), Uber, pay as you drive, city
logistics concepts, or satellite navigation (services), or the maglev train and charging facilities (infrastructure). But many
candidate innovations fail. And if they succeed, they might have important impacts on society not only the travellers or
companies transporting goods, but also peoples being exposed to noise and pollution, and companies selling vehicles or proving
services. And such changes might be relevant for policy makers.
In this course you will learn about factors important for the success or failure of candidate innovations, and the societal impacts
of these innovations.
learning_objectives:
By the end of this course, you should be able to
LO1: Explain the main frameworks that describe the success or failure of innovations.
LO2: Explain the main pathways (e.g., via transport resistance, location choices, travel behaviour aspects) that link transport and
logistics innovations and their societal impacts (on the environment, accessibility, safety, health).
LO3: Analyse the success and failure factors of candidate transport and logistics innovations using a combination of frameworks
from the literature.
LO4: Build a conceptual model that illustrates the societal impacts (on the environment, accessibility, safety, health) of candidate
transport and logistics innovations.

description:
System Theory, Object Orientation, Discrete Event System Specification, Multi-Formalism Simulation, Distributed Simulation,
Real-Time Simulation, Multi-Paradigm Simulation, Multi-Resolution Simulation, and Simulation Language selection will be the
core topics of the course. After an introduction to system theory, the inner working of simulation environments will be illustrated
on the basis of the DEVS, DESS, and DTSS formalisms. Then, possible integrating of the different formalisms will be shown.
Several special topics will be taught, based on the latest research in simulation. This material will be illustrated in intensive and
interactive courses.
In addition to the lecture topics, several other simulation topics will be studied by groups of students, who will write a scientific
paper, and present their findings in class. These topics can be focused on the MSc program that the students participate in;
special topics to study are available for TIL, CoSEM, EPA, Computer Science, and other students.
Finally, groups of students will study a simulation package in-depth and discuss the commonalities and differences with other
packages. Again, the package chosen can be targeted at the MSc program of the students. TIL students can, e.g. study a package
that is more aimed at logistics and transport, CoSEM students can focus on a package that is used in systems design, whereas
EPA students can focus on a package used in policy analysis. Most packages can be made available for use from home.
This course requires active participation and contains group work.

Experienced speakers, from consultancy organizations (s.a. Accenture), game designers and universities, will give lectures on
history, future, design, typology and facilitation of SG. (We will discuss the role of computers and video games, but emphasis is
NOT on technology!) We will have ample opportunity to try out a number of (role-playing, board etc.) games that hold powerful
messages about decision-making and management. Most of the work will be done in small teams, in which students will develop
their own (non-digital) game to support a real-life or mock up case of policy/decision-making or organization and management.
In a small group, you will also work on a scientific question related to game design.
learning_objectives:
After completion of this course the student will have acquired knowledge and insights about:
The history, backgrounds, key-concepts, formats and applications of simulation games.
After completion of this course the student will be able to:
1. Design a (prototype) of a simulation game to be used for learning, research or intervention
2. Apply a game design cycle (or systematic design steps)
3. Define, conceptualize and construct the various game components
4. Facilitate simple simulation games

description:
A transition to sustainable energy is needed for our climate and welfare. In this course, you will learn how to assess the potential
for energy reduction and the potential of renewable energy sources like hydropower, wind, solar and biomass. Assessing the
energy balance of a country is important to understand the opportunities and challenges for the transition to sustainable energy.
Some basic principles of energy transition models will be discussed. The physical and chemical principles that determine the
impact of our energy consumption on the earth's climate is briefly discussed, as well. This course gives an overview of the most
important renewable energy sources, the challenges to incorporate those in the electric network and the need for storage. Youll
learn how to integrate these sources in an energy system, like an electricity network and take an engineering approach to look for
solutions and design a 100% sustainable energy system.
This is a core course in the Sustainable Energy Technology MSc program.
learning_objectives:
After this course students are able to ...
(cid:9)make simple estimations of the impact of planet earth's albedo, radiative forcing, greenhouse gas emissions on the climate of the
planet (temperature, sea levels).
(cid:9)Using physical principles you will be able to estimate the use of energy in transport, building and manufacturing.
(cid:9)Using physical principles you will be able to estimate the generation of Renewable Energy. How much can you generate from all
the different sources? (Hydropower, Wind Energy, Solar Energy, Biomass, Tidal Energy, Wave Energy)
(cid:9)Using physical principles you will be able to estimate the power density and energy density of various storage technologies?
(cid:9)You will be able to analyze large scale energy infrastructure using energy balances and identify corresponding climate effects of
such energy infrastructure.
(cid:9)You will be able to analyze the capacity factor, system efficiency, energy pay back time, circularity aspects of energy systems.
(cid:9)You will understand how policies can stimulate the use of renewable energy and improve energy efficiency?
(cid:9)You will be able to design a 100% sustainable energy system.
(cid:9)You will understand the technological principles and challenges for various Renewable Energy technologies

description:
This course is a general introduction to energy economics. In this course, you learn the essentials of how actors in the energy
system make economic decisions, when markets work well and when they may fail, and what options the government has to
remedy market failures. Specifically, the following topics are addressed:
(cid:9)Introduction to energy (electricity) markets: perfect competition; oligopoly
(cid:9)Rational (and irrational) market behaviour; ABM ?
(cid:9)Investment decision making; LCOE
(cid:9)Opportunity costing / discounting; NPV; IRR; discount rate
(cid:9)Markets, (perfect) competition and market failure (esp. externalities & lock-in)
(cid:9)Private costs, external cost and social cost; empirical evidence (related to energy)
(cid:9)LCOE; discounting; private discount rate; IRR and NPV
(cid:9)Social cost-benefit analysis; social discount rate

description:
This course is an introduction to mathematical optimization modelling applied to diverse problems in planning and operating
energy systems, in particular energy systems with a high share of variable (weather-dependent) wind and solar generation. We
will go from a solid theoretical grounding in formulating different kinds of optimization problems, to practical strategies to solve
them under real-world conditions. The course covers linear, nonlinear, and mixed-integer optimization, as well as game theory in
the context of multi-actor decision problems. We will use Matlab to formulate and solve optimization problems.
This course is the first course in the SET programme.
learning_objectives:
After completing the course, you should be able to:
- LO1: Explain the challenges in planning and operating renewable energy systems and the role of mathematical optimisation in
addressing these challenges
- LO2: Formulate and solve linear, mixed-integer, and non-linear optimisation problems
- LO3: Apply different methods to deal with parametric uncertainty in optimisation
- LO4: Determine and justify the choice of an optimisation approach to formulate an energy system decision problem
- LO5: Explain how formulating multi-actor decision problems is different from single-actor decision problems
- LO6: Formulate and solve optimisation problems using Matlab

description:
Intelligent Electrical Power Grids - a.k.a. Smart Grids - are the "smartified" version of our electricity infrastructure. By adding
controls, communication, and other digital elements these grids are expected to be more flexible, robust, efficient, and capable in
order to satisfy the requirements of the future: hosting more renewable sources, catering for an active demand side, or
implementing flexible peer-to-peer energy markets.
Working with Smart Grids requires knowledge in a variety of disciplines out of electrical engineering, computer science, and
mathematics. Of great importance is modeling and simulation, since Smart Grids show a level of complexity and heterogeneity
that often can not be covered by analytical methods. In this course you will learn how to describe and assess a Smart Grid,
mainly by using numerical tools.
You will use various modeling and simulation tools to investigate the properties of smart power grids. Each practical results in a
(very) short report. In the end, an electronic exam will be done.
This course is part of the Power track of the SET master and can also be chosen by EE master students.
Understanding of power flow is expected. Slides and exercises to check if you are up for it are provide on Brightspace.
learning_objectives:
After this course students are able to
- create a demand/supply matching system, to
- model and simulate a smart grid, to
- specify the design requirements of a SCADA system, and to
- analyse cyber security threats, threat vectors, and vulnerabilities of ITOT smart grid systems.

description:
In this course you will learn about the following aspects of biomass conversion based on thermo-chemical conversion
technologies.
- Biomass Characterisation (biomass types, properties, analyses)
- Pretreatment (harvesting, size reduction, drying, torrefaction)
- Thermochemical conversion (combustion, gasification and pyrolysis; reactor types)
- Transportation fuels / biorefinery (syngas conversion, economics)
- Process design (structured design approach)
learning_objectives:
During this course, the students will obtain knowledge of and insight into energy conversion technologies based on biomass
thermo-chemical conversion processes for a wide variety of applications, like supply of power, heat and fuels. They will be
offered practical problems to solve and projects to perform in this area.
These main learning objectives can be divided into several smaller learning objectives:
1) The student has knowledge on the typical biomass composition, related properties (like e.g. heating value, ash melting
behaviour) and can critically identify and select fuel characterization techniques.
2) The student is able to identify and perform basic capacity calculations concerning thermo-chemical biomass conversion
systems for small and larger scale (combined) heat and power generation as well as systems for transportation fuel production.
3) The student is able to set up reaction equations (stoichiometry) for a wide range of energy supply related fuel conversion
processes.
4) The student can set up and perform heat and mass balance calculations regarding single phase and simple multi-phase biomass
thermo-chemical conversion reactors and extended (downstream) systems for power, heat and fuels generation.
5) The student knows how to perform basic ideal gas phase chemical reaction equilibrium calculations to calculate product
compositions and extents of reactions given initial reaction mixture composition, pressure and temperature.
6) The student can understand and describe reaction kinetic expressions and also apply them in order to solve (design) problems
related to the conversion of fuels and the formation of emission components.
7) The student demonstrates good knowledge of mass and heat transfer mechanisms and phenomena applied to the chemical
conversion of both liquid and solid biomass (derived) fuels.
8) The student can derive equations for idealised model reactors (well-stirred reactor and plug flow reactor concepts) and apply
these simplified reactor concepts to solve engineering problems related to the thermo-chemical conversion of biomass fuels, in
particular combustion, gasification and pyrolysis.
9) The student is able to perform calculations concerning the conversion of small particles; important in this respect is the
identification of the regime of conversion. Related dimensionless numbers such as the Thiele Modulus and the Biot number are
key indicators in this respect.
10) The student is able to understand the basics of thermo-chemical conversion processes and to translate this into designing and
evaluating such (sometimes hybrid) systems, including their economic evaluation based on characteristic parameters like NPV,
POT, and ROI.
11) The student demonstrates good communication skills, both oral and written, concerning presentation of (applied) scientific
results.

description:
In a renewable energy future energy storage is an additional necessary means to match the supply and demand of energy.
- Week 1: Future energy generation systems, the combination of sources on a large scale.
Group work 1: program in Matlab a numerical model for energy generation, with flexible input of PV, solar heat, wind, hydro,
biofuel
- Week 2: Future energy use possibilities: look into current typical use patterns of the different sectors, and look into possible
changes: electrification, different sources, etc.
Group work 2: program in Matlab typical use patterns for the different sectors
- Week 3: Estimate the possibilities for 'demand response' in the different sectors and program this in Matlab. Deduce the
resulting demand for short term and long term storage. Determine the demand for transport of energy and estimate possible
transport losses.
Group work 3: program in Matlab the different magnitudes for demand response, short and long storage throughout the year.
- Week 4: Storage methods introduction, pumped hydro, mechanical, compressed air, deployment possibilities.
Group work 4: calculate different factors for energy density, capacity, timescale of storage. Investigate approximate efficiency.
- Week 5: Thermal storage, high T and low T. Combined heat and power possibilities.
Group work 5: Investigate energy densities, efficiencies, capacities, exergies.
- Week 6: Biomass and biofuels, future prospects for storage. Introduction to scalable chemical energy storage methods: batteries
and fuels. What would electrification of the chemical industry mean.
Group work: investigate biofuel resources, calculate efficiencies and compare to solar PV and electrolysis numbers.
- Week 7: Hand in report and model. Group presentations of the model calculations (where each group has different boundary
conditions). Discuss how the boundary conditions influence the outcome of the storage demand.
learning_objectives:
At the end of the lectures and group work the students should be able to:
-(cid:9)Reproduce and reflect on the role of storage in a renewable energy based society.
-(cid:9)Explain how different timescales for energy storage are relevant for the future system.
-(cid:9)List and explain the different storage solutions in terms of typical energy density, cost and efficiency.
-(cid:9)Tell about the different drivers for energy conversion including demand for storage, and demand for transport of energy.
-(cid:9)Reflect on the energy efficiency of intermediate storage.

description:
Hydrogen is a vital element in the energy transition. While sustainable energy sources such as solar and wind plants will power
the planet, this energy needs to be converted in chemical bonds to provide storage, fuel and resources to our future energy
system. Hydrogen is the most simple chemical bond that can be made by (electro)chemistry. Hence, we will discuss the various
(electro-)chemical ways that hydrogen can be produced and discuss the main impediments for the implementation of this
technology. Once the hydrogen is produced it will need to be stored and converted. Hence, we will discuss the basics of different
storage methods: as a gas, liquid, adsorbed or absorbed inside appropriate solids. Furthermore, the use of hydrogen as a fuel in
several types of fuel cells will be discussed.
learning_objectives:
After this course students:
(cid:9)Students are able to distinguish the various sustainable methods to produce hydrogen, assess their pro/cons and describe their
operation in thermodynamic terms.
(cid:9)Students have a basic understanding of the physical nature of hydrogen and are able to assess the various ways of storing it.
(cid:9)Students have a basic understanding of various fuel cell technologies and are able to assess their efficiency and describe their
operation in thermodynamic terms.

description:
Hydrogen is a vital element in the energy transition. While sustainable energy sources such as solar and wind plants will power
the planet, this energy needs to be converted in chemical bonds to provide storage, fuel and resources to our future energy
system. Hydrogen is the most simple chemical bond that can be made by (electro)chemistry. Hence, we will discuss the various
(electro-)chemical ways that hydrogen can be produced and discuss the main impediments for the implementation of this
technology. Once the hydrogen is produced it will need to be stored and converted. Hence, we will discuss the basics of different
storage methods: as a gas, liquid, adsorbed or absorbed inside appropriate solids. Furthermore, the use of hydrogen as a fuel in
several types of fuel cells will be discussed.

operation in thermodynamic terms.
(cid:9)Students have a basic understanding of the physical nature of hydrogen and are able to assess the various ways of storing it.
(cid:9)Students have a basic understanding of various fuel cell technologies and are able to assess their efficiency and describe their
operation in thermodynamic terms.

description:
This course covers the principles of power conversion with switch-mode circuits with sustainable energy applications in mind.
The basic circuits of power electronics are explained, including ac-dc converters (diode rectifiers), dc-dc converters (non-
isolated) and dc-ac converters (inverters). Issues specific to power electronics including pulse width modulation, methods of
analysis, voltage distortion, power quality and commonly used power semiconductor switches are treated.
learning_objectives:
To get acquainted with applications of power electronics; to understand the principles of power electronics; to get an overview of
power electronic circuits; to sketch and explain circuit diagram and their specific waveforms and functionalities; To be able to
select appropriate circuits for specific power electronics applications.

description:
This course focusses on the technology of (hybrid) electric vehicles and its charging technology
(cid:9)Tank to Wheel, Well to Tank, Well to Wheel efficiencies and emission estimation for conventional, hybrid and fully electric
vehicles based on energy source for propulsion.
(cid:9)Types, operational principles, advantages and disadvantages of vehicle architectures: internal combustion engine; micro, mild
and full hybrids (series, parallel, series-parallel), plug-in hybrids, full electrics, fuel cell vehicles;
(cid:9)Vehicle load forces & dynamics, mechanical transmission components, power and energy consumption, drive cycles, battery
sizing and electric vehicle range, MPGe, planetary gears as a power-split, regenerative braking.
(cid:9)Principles of battery operation, battery types, the key performance parameters of batteries, from cell to battery pack, charge-
discharge curves, battery and thermal management systems.
(cid:9)Fundamentals and types of electric machine drives used in electric cars: its characteristics, efficiency, basics of motor control.
(cid:9)Basics of power electronic converters used in electric cars and chargers, topologies and control.
(cid:9)Charging methods of EVs: AC charging, DC charging, vehicle-to-grid technology, wireless charging, battery swap; charging
time estimation, effects of fast charging on battery; Smart charging of EVs and vehicle-to-grid, communication protocols for
smart charging.
(cid:9)Modelling and investigating the performance of the electric vehicle drivetrain using quasi-static simulation in
MATLAB/Simulink.
(cid:9)Case study of EV: Toyota Prius HEV, Tesla Model S, Porsche Taycan, Audi e-tron, Hyundai Ioniq 5
The course will have a design project where students have to form teams to design their own EV by making choices for the
vehicle drivetrain and corresponding charging technology. Emphasis will be on justifying and quantifying the technological
design choices including drivetrain architecture, well-to-wheel efficiency and emissions, energy storage, power electronics, type
of motor and charging method.
learning_objectives:
The goal of this course is to educate students to design and evaluate various (hybrid) electric vehicles with respect to their
performance, efficiency, sustainability, charging methodologies and potential for grid support.
At the end of the course, the students should be able to:
(cid:9)Evaluate the performance of hybrids (series, parallel, series-parallel), plug-in hybrid and fully electric drivetrain architectures
based on power and energy consumption, efficiency, driving range, well-to-wheel emissions and charging time.
(cid:9)Explain the design trade-offs in the energy sources (battery, fuel cell, super capacitors) and motors used in electric vehicles based
on the key performance indicators like efficiency, energy and/or power density, lifetime, and control.
(cid:9)Analyse various charging technologies for electric vehicles (conductive, inductive or battery swap) based on power electronics
converters used, type of the charger (AC Vs DC), connector types, power levels, and modes.
(cid:9)Investigate the performance of the (hybrid) electric vehicle drivetrain using quasi-static modelling and simulation in
MATLAB/Simulink.
(cid:9)Design a (hybrid) electric drivetrain by sizing and making the relevant choice of the electric machine, internal combustion
engine, energy source (batteries, fuel cells, etc.), power electronic converters, transmissions components, and charging
technology for a given vehicle specification.

description:
Depleting fossil fuels and environmental concerns force us to change the way we produce our goods. The transition of the
chemical industry to becoming sustainable represents one of the major challenges to be faced in the 21st century. Catalytic
reactions will increasingly substitute the existing energy- and resource-intensive production procedures; hence reducing or
preventing toxic pollutants. Biotechnology will play a major role in this transition and complement advanced chemical
production technologies.
This course will highlight the emerging role of catalysis in the chemical industry. A major focus will lie on biotechnological
production of chemicals (fermentation processes, isolated enzymes). These methods will be related to their chemocatalytic
counterparts. Thus, ample examples including the underlying mechanistic principles - of bio- and chemocatalytic processes will
be discussed. Finally, the emerging field of renewable feedstocks will be discussed not only from a chemical standpoint, but also
on socioeconomical and ecological grounds. The 12 Principles of Green Chemistry will serve as guideline to assess the scope
and limitations of the examples discussed.
learning_objectives:
After attending this course the student will:
(1) have detailed knowledge of sustainable catalysts (enzyme- and chemo-catalysis)
(2) know industrial examples of sustainable manufacturing practice
(3) be able to use the 12 Principles of Green Chemistry to assess the sustainability of a given process
(4) be able to critically assess the purport of green claims

description:
"Learn the fundamentals of the MATLAB scripting language and model-based design using Simulink"
Get acquainted with MATLAB and Simulink though a series of interactive lectures focusing on developing real-world
programming skills and insight. A series of "activities" during lectures and weekly homework get you to increase your "hands-
on" experience. Get to focus on common pitfalls and mistakes and how to avoid them. Get exposed to "good" programming style
guidelines so that others can better understand and further work with, or modify your code and designs. You get to practice in a
mid-term mini project and demonstrate your newly acquired skills in a final mini project.
learning_objectives:
After having passed this course...
- You will be able to install and run MATLAB/SIMULINK in either Windows, Mac OS, Linux, or Android operating systems.
- You will be able to operate MATLAB/SIMULINK, at least basically, either by the graphical user interface or command-line
interface.
- You will be able to develop, write and evaluate simple programs that run in MATLAB/SIMULINK.
- You will be able to import evaluate and export data in native formats and other common data formats.
- You will be able to create visualization aids (figures, plots, graphs, charts) that comply with standards in engineering and
science.
- You will be able to choose and apply the right code and/or model blocks to guarantee compatibility with specific versions of
MATLAB/SIMULINK.
- You will be able to avoid, identify and correct common pitfalls and mistakes in writing and running code.
- You will be able to follow basic design and programming guidelines that make MATLAB/SIMULINK programs easier to read
and work with.

description:
Internship SET is a three-month (15 ECTS) project on a sustainable energy engineering topic performed at a company or
institute, either in the Netherlands or abroad. It is not allowed to do an internship which is longer than three months. The final
report needs to be written and handed in within three months after the start of the internship. General guidelines are that it should
concern a design, model, system integration or methodology implementation, or an experimental study relevant for the company
involved and within the Profile Cluster. Literature study can only be a minor part of the internship.
When carrying out Internship SET (SET3822) at a company or institute, the following conditions apply:
The student joins in with the company or institute culture in general, including sharing the company-established balance
between on-site and online work.
The student joins in with the day-to-day running of the company or institute similar to regular employees. This includes having
regular consultation and interaction with colleagues and manager(s), and use of and access to the company-specific resources
and tools applicable to the internship. Such resources and tools can be physical/on-site (e.g. measurement equipment, company
machines and infrastructure) as well as virtual (online, software tools, databases, ...).
NB: Internship SET (SET3822) can never be part of a Graduation Project (SET3901) and it is not allowed to carry out both your
internship and your thesis at the same company.
Detailed information on projects, procedures and application is available on the Brightspace course SET3822.
learning_objectives:
Learn about sustainable energy projects in a professional environment, and apply sustainable energy related knowledge on a
(new or persistent) problem relevant for the company or institute. Produce a project report that gives useful answers to the initial
questions of the company and that gives the TU Delft supervisor sufficiently detailed insight in the project and its results. You
will also be required to write an experience report. Guidelines for writing your reports can be found on Brightspace course
SET3822.
There are three main educational goals for the Internship SET (SET3822):
I. Profession related aspects:
Insight into the profession of an engineer in Sustainable Energy Technology.
Insight into the duties and the responsibilities of an engineer in a company.
II. Social-psychological aspects:
Learning to move in another culture (both within and outside the company).
Dealing with another language for a longer period.
Gaining insight into the position of the company with respect to comparable companies.
III. Professional knowledge and skills related aspects:
Learning to apply the gained knowledge and skills in a situation different from the (own) university situation.
Learning to acquire new knowledge and skills that are necessary to meet the requirements for the Internship SET (SET3822).

description:
The graduation project (SET3901) worth 45 EC is performed under supervision of one of the research groups affiliated with the
Profile Cluster chosen by the student.
In the Graduation Project a student works independently on a research project. Important is that system integration is addressed
in the Graduation Project. The topic of this project can be defined in several ways:
- A specialized topic addressing a specific component of the energy system within one profile (Wind Energy, Solar Energy,
Biomass Energy, Power, Storage, Economics & Society). In that case the relation with the energy system must also be
demonstrated in the report.
- A topic on system integration within one profile (Wind Energy, Solar Energy, Biomass Energy, Power, Storage, Economics &
Society, Electric Mobility).
- A topic on system integration across two or more profiles in a combined project. In that case one of the profiles will take the
lead, but the student will have supervisors from all profiles.
The research project encompasses the following activities:
- Literature study, problem formulation and planning;
- Practical and theoretical work in one of the research groups, including interpretation and evaluation of the results;
- Oral and written presentation of the work.
For procedures see the course on Brightspace => MSc SET Thesis Project EEMCS. This also holds for graduation projects partly
carried out with external partners.
The Graduation Project is carried out at Delft University of Technology. If needed for the successful completion of the research,
it is allowed to carry out the Graduation Project at a company. This has to be approved by the profile leader of the Board of
Examiners of MSc SET, and supported by a written motivation from the supervisor. The Graduation Project always needs to be
carried out according to MSc SET guidelines of Delft University of Technology.

description:
Scope: Due to the growing interest in sustainable energy production, the Department of Geoscience and Engineering offers a
course on geothermal energy. This introductory course presents the fundamentals of geothermal resource exploitation. Students
will gain a general understanding of what a geothermal resource is and of the basic steps in their economic exploitation,
including lifetime analysis, characterization and design of a geothermal reservoir, reservoir engineering, plant design and
construction, basics of the operation and maintenance of geothermal systems, and geothermal field management, as well as some
environmental aspects.
Contents:
- Introduction to geothermal energy
- Geology and geomechanics
- Reservoir characterization
- Design of a geothermal system
- Geothermal reservoir engineering
- Numerical modeling of geothermal doublets
- Techno-economic assessment of geothermal systems
learning_objectives:
After successfully completing this course you will be able to:
Classify geothermal systems based on their different geological settings
Describe and apply geomechanical principles related to geothermal systems
Describe solute and heat transfer in porous media by mathematical equations and explain their role in different geothermal
systems (Darcy flow, conductive and convective heat transfer , diffusion and advection equations)
Develop a 2D and 3D Finite Element (FE) model in COMSOL describing a direct use geothermal system by implementing real
world data
Design a prototype geothermal system:
-Choose the appropriate location and well configuration
-Assess the system lifetime, power, generated energy and stochastic economic output
-Justify your geothermal development choices from an energy, engineering and economic point of view"
faculty: Electrical Engineering, Mathematics and Computer Science

description:
Als docent ben je nooit uitgeleerd. In dit vak hebben we het over professionele ontwikkeling van jezelf als docent in een school.
Je doet enkele opdrachten die inzicht geven in je professionele identiteit. Daarnaast werk je aan het realiseren van een innovatie
op je (stage)school. Daarbij ligt de nadruk op het proces van innoveren en de samenwerking met je collegas.
Dit vak wordt vormgegeven als een Professionele Leergemeenschap (PLG). Er is daardoor veel ruimte voor uitwisseling over
onder meer professionele identiteit, het vormgeven van innovaties en richting geven aan je eigen ontwikkeling.
learning_objectives:
De student kan aspecten van zijn/haar eigen professionele identiteit beschrijven.
De student kan de professionele identiteit van collega-docenten beschrijven op basis van een interview.
De student kan reflecteren op het proces van innoveren in de school en dit relateren aan de professionele identiteit van zichzelf
en de collegas die betrokken zijn bij de innovatie.
De student is in staat constructief bij te dragen aan een professionele leergemeenschap met peers.

description:
This course will take you in the realm of the departments community of practice: C-Lab. You will take part in de the dynamics
of the design process (as part of our design-based research) that is carried out within this real practice. The main objective is to
analyse and support the way professionals take decision upon their communication in real collaborative networks for
transformative innovations. Within teams of students with various disciplinary backgrounds you will take part, observe and
analyse the case owners real practice from various theoretical perspectives (e.g. science communication, marketing, responsible
research and innovation, corporate communication and branding) that fit to the multi-levelled and multi-staged reality of the case
owner. The design method and its according tools will help you to co-design with the professionals at stake a decisions strategy
and decision support tool that will support their future development. By using continuously the links between technology &
society, communication theory & practice, ratio & art you will learn to feel comfortable to generate ideas for the future that not
necessarily are brilliant from the start but support all members of the C-Lab to think again and/or further.
learning_objectives:
is able to understand and describe challenges in decision making in the dynamic collaborative network of a real case by making
use of theories on decisions making in collaborative settings
understands system thinking and design thinking and the direct conceptual and methodological link with complexity
can design a decision support strategy and an according supportive tool that support professionals in the collaborative
transformative innovation network to make adaptive decisions upon their communication
has knowledge of design methods
feel comfortable in lingering thinking between technology & society, and communication theory & practice, ratio & art
can reflect on design thinking as a mind set for adaptive professionals through which one is able and dares to use theory,
experience, creativity and intuition together as various sources of knowledge
can apply design methods and tools in collaboration with fellow students and commissioner in the setting of a community of
practice

description:
This course gives an introduction to theories from the fields of Communication Science and Team Science.
Communication Science is an important building block of the field of Science Communication, and crucial for designing
communication tools for innovation. It is important that you familiarize yourself with distinct theories of Communication
Science that can help you to understand what communication is and how people communicate with each other. These theories
are centred around the topics of transdisciplinary learning, social learning, and decision-making.
Theories from Team Science are used to give you a theoretical overview of how teamwork is understood from a scientific
perspective, with the aim that you can reflect on your own teamwork throughout the Master's and potentially make it more
effective.
Therefore this introductory course is designed to give you a strong theoretical basis for the Master CDI. Next to this, through
analyzing a case related to innovation/technology in small interdisciplinary teams, you will learn to apply these theories and
experience teamwork at the same time, while you also prepare for the exam, which is mainly focusing on higher-level learning
skills: understanding and application of the theories.
learning_objectives:
After finishing this course you are able to
- define the basic building block of scientific theories
- understand communication and collaboration theories
- analyze STEM-related cases from a communication science perspective
- evaluate which communication and collaboration theories are suitable for the given cases
- apply communication and collaboration theories in given technical/innovation contexts
- write case analysis reports including the theories applied
- elaborate your own teamwork based on the collaboration theories

description:
In the context of the changing dynamics within and between science and society, it becomes increasingly important to
understand the communication processes at several interfaces: communication between scientists from different disciplines,
between science and the public, and between science and their stakeholders, like representatives of business, unions,
government, the media, and environmental and community interest groups.
In this course we will explore the landscape of science communication. We will examine relationships between various
stakeholders and analyze the way they communicate. We will also try to figure out why communication sometimes fails, by
focusing on specific cases in practice and view them from different perspectives.
This course also examines current developments in both science and technology and in the science communication field from a
theoretical perspective. Scientific papers will provide you with the theories and models to analyze current debates, help you form
your own opinion and to substantiate it well.
At the end of the course, we focus on the science communication professional. We discuss tasks, dilemmas and challenges. One
of the assignments is aimed at sketching your own future role in science communication.

Most of you will take this course at the end of your masters programme. To enable you to bridge the gap between your current
position as a student and your future career - as a science communication professional, communication engineer or researcher -
we offer you the course Personal Professional Development.
Central in this course is the following question: what do you need to grow and develop personally and professionally in a
dynamic context? In this course you will have the chance to search for answers to this question.
In this course we will map the current state of literature on several key concepts related to personal professional development,
such as Professional Identity, Agency and Adaptive expertise. The Insights from literature, from guest speakers and CDI-alumni,
discussions with team mates, (peer group) feedback and reflection will help to draw a personal professional development plan
and find answers to questions on your personal professional growth.

This course teaches you how to set up a social scientific research project. The content of the course covers qualitative and
quantitative research methods, including e.g. interviews, surveys and observation techniques. During the lectures, we will discuss
the implementation of such relevant social scientific research methods in practical research studies within the SEC (Science
Education & Communication) department. In collaboration with the SEC staff, you write a research proposal for a research
project that contributes to actual, ongoing SEC research themes. During this course, you will work in groups to write a research
project proposal and plan the actual research. As a continuation, in the Research methods in Social Sciences part 2 (SL3531)
course, you will carry out this research project by applying all concepts and knowledge learned during this course.
learning_objectives:
At the end of this course:
- You can describe the importance and the benefits of research methods in social sciences and give examples of their use.
- You can define the different research methods used in social sciences (qualitative, quantitative and mixed methods).
- You can identify valid, ethical, and reliable research and incorporate these issues into the research design.
- You will be able to design a social scientific research project
- You can formulate relevant and adequate research questions.
- You can perform literature research on a given social scientific research problem.
- Based on the scientific literature you will be able to formulate a theoretical framework for the given research topic.
- You can choose from the different social scientific methods to answer your research question, and justify the theory as well as
the methodological decisions, including sampling and measurement.
- You will be able to create a detailed time plan for your research.
- You can write a coherent Research project proposal.
- You can keep a learning diary/logbook, registering your key ideas and questions, the ways you searched for answers, the
research process (including the literature search) and the decisions made throughout the course.
- You are able to maintain a responsible and reactive work relationship with the case owner.
- You are able to read critically.
- You are able to work in teams.

description:
This course will provide you with insights in real strategic (science)communication challenges that come along with large
innovation projects and transitions. You will learn how to analyse such a case from various theoretical perspectives of corporate
communication and branding, and apply these insights in a communication policy process and its according strategy that
improves the case commissioners communication practice. Within teams of students with various disciplinary backgrounds you
will apply design thinking in order to get grip on the case itself and to create direct links between technology & society, and
(science)communication theory & practice. The design method and its according tools will support you in designing a strategy
that has an immediate fit with reality and supports the case owner future development. Together with the team, the commissioner
and the CDI staff you will slowly but surely start to work in our so called Community of Practice.
During the lectures, the various possible communication policy and strategy models will be considered. As a course participant
you will link organizational strategy to communication strategy and you will learn how to use and consider terms such as
reputation', 'integrated communication, brand' and 'identity. On the basis of such theory you will be required to forge a link with
actual practice by examining several particular cases.
Professionals in the field will be asked to explain how, in practice, the communication policy of their organisation can be shaped
while also indicating where the main problem areas lie. In the process, the kinds of questions addressed will be: How can the
complexity and uncertainty of goals and processes be reconciled?, How can policy and strategy be embedded in the
organisation?, How can the ethical norms and values that fit in with the organisation be utilised?
learning_objectives:
demonstrates mastery in theory of science communication policy and strategy
understands the complexity of (science)communication challenges in practices and is able to reflect on this from a theoretical
perspective based on corporate communication and branding theories
understands the complex relationship that exists between the theoretical and practical sides of science communication policy and
strategy as a fundament for the design of a communication strategy
practice their communication skills in media presentation
understands the significance of science communication policy and strategy in the context of collaboration in (transformative)
innovations

description:
The SEC/CDI research group studies, designs and develops communication-based methods and tools that support professionals
who work in innovation environments. This support always includes a communication angle: better collaboration strategies,
setting up a 'community of practice' or 'living lab' for multi (or trans) disciplinary collaboration, communication skills training,
developing branding strategies, etc. Such tools can support the development of innovation quality, and by extension possibly its
commercial value for organizations that develop these (technical) innovations.
In this course you will explore ways to 'valorize' innovation, i.e. to transform research outcomes into a 'something' that is socially
or commercially 'interesting', though a strategy for the innovator for the coming 6-12 months, in which innovation and
communication become more intertwined.
You develop a strategy (in the form of an advisory report) for an 'innovator' (case study), keeping various stakeholder groups in
mind. You combine insights from innovation studies, science communication and marketing theory to develop this plan from a
theoretical basis.

This course will help you to reflect and develop on what knowledge, strategy, dynamics, uncertainty and adaptability (the 4
building blocks of our curriculum) means for you as a person. This is important since in your future professional life you
certainly need to deal and cope with other disciplines and practices. You might need to integrate professionals thoughts, ideas
and knowledge into a collaboration process on a human measure. Therefore, it is important to have a deep experience of this
integration process yourself.
In four consecutive sessions you will gain this deep experience by reflecting on how what you have learned affects you
personally. Through this you will continuously develop your personal learning trajectory throughout the curriculum. Whereas in
the various courses of CDIs curriculum the reflection and development is much more content or method based, the 4 sessions
will be guided by the lecturer and a personal logbook is the guidebook throughout the process that you create yourself. And with
every single step your Coiling abilities will increase. Each session (and its accompanying courses) will challenge you on the
different sources of understanding prominent in the CDI curriculum: theory, experience, creativity, and intuition. The Coiling
course is strongly connected to the Internship and Personal and Professional Development course at the end of the first year.
Why Coiling? COIL is the name of CDIs Community of Practice in which professionals, students and CDI staff work closely
together. Within these processes of co-creation the continuous looping between theory & practice, science, technology & society,
ratio & intuition is of main importance.
learning_objectives:
After this course:
You are able to be open to other disciplines and practices and integrate these when needed to solve complex issues using
personal experience, intuition, creativity and theory.
You are able to critically reflect on yourself, as a baseline for current on-going personal and future professional development,
and can apply this in the development of a personal learning trajectory.
You are able to support others in the process of self-reflection and the personal development thereof.

description:
Onderwijskunde is een vakgebied dat gericht is op het begrijpen en verbeteren van onderwijs. Het heeft betrekking op
leerprocessen en interactie binnen en buiten de klas, op de docent, de schoolorganisatie, maar ook op beleid en bestuur van het
onderwijs. De functie van onderwijskunde in de opleiding van leraren is dat de docenten in opleiding (DIOs) zich eigen maken
wat toepasbaar is uit deze wetenschappelijke discipline bij het lesgeven van alle dag en om hen te helpen een onderzoekende
houding aan te nemen. In de colleges van het vak Onderwijskunde passeren daarom onderwerpen de revue die vanuit een
onderwijskundig en pedagogisch (opvoedkundig) perspectief een licht werpen op de onderwijspraktijk. Dat betreft ook
onderwerpen die niet direct verbonden zijn aan het ontwikkelen van je eigen lespraktijk, maar wel wezenlijk zijn voor je begrip
van het onderwijs en de schoolorganisatie.
Onderwijskunde is een theoretisch vak dat je de gelegenheid geeft te ontdekken en uit te diepen wat zich in het hoofd van
leerlingen, in de klas en op school afspeelt en de rol jij daarbij als docent speelt. Onderwijskunde is een kaderstellend vak waarin
basiskennis op het gebied van onderwijzen en leren aan bod komt.
learning_objectives:
In Onderwijskunde staan de volgende leerdoelen centraal:
1. Je hebt kennis van belangrijke theorieën in relatie tot interpersoonlijk docentgedrag.
2. Je hebt kennis van belangrijke theorieën uit de adolescentiepsychologie die relevant zijn voor het onderwijs.
3. Je hebt kennis over de pedagogische opdracht van de school.
4. Je hebt kennis over de belangrijkste leer- en motivatietheorieën (en hun ontstaansgeschiedenis) en je bent in staat deze
theorieën aan elkaar en aan actuele onderwijssituaties en -ontwikkelingen te verbinden.
5. Je hebt kennis over hoe leerlingen leren, in termen van motivatie, leeractiviteiten en leeroriëntaties en je kunt deze kennis
koppelen aan de belangrijkste leertheorieën.
6. Je kunt non-verbale en verbale gedragingen van de docent waarnemen en je bevindingen schriftelijk presenteren.
7. Je kunt met behulp van het hardop-denkmethode de denkstappen en metacognitieve activiteiten van de leerlingen in kaart
brengen.
8. Je kunt een ontwikkelingsgebied van de adolescentie in kaart brengen en dit verbinden aan het lesgeven en de begeleiding van
de adolescent.
9. Je kunt een onderwijskundig onderwerp in kaart brengen en aan de hand van diverse bronnen je bevindingen schriftelijk
presenteren

leerprocessen en interactie binnen en buiten de klas, op de docent, de schoolorganisatie, maar ook op beleid en bestuur van het
onderwijs. De functie van onderwijskunde in de opleiding van leraren is dat de docenten in opleiding (DIOs) zich eigen maken
wat toepasbaar is uit deze wetenschappelijke discipline bij het lesgeven van alle dag en om hen te helpen een onderzoekende
houding aan te nemen. In de colleges van het vak Onderwijskunde passeren daarom onderwerpen de revue die vanuit een
onderwijskundig en pedagogisch (opvoedkundig) perspectief een licht werpen op de onderwijspraktijk. Dat betreft ook
onderwerpen die niet direct verbonden zijn aan het ontwikkelen van je eigen lespraktijk, maar wel wezenlijk zijn voor je begrip
van het onderwijs en de schoolorganisatie.
Onderwijskunde is een theoretisch vak dat je de gelegenheid geeft te ontdekken en uit te diepen wat zich in het hoofd van
leerlingen, in de klas en op school afspeelt en de rol jij daarbij als docent speelt. Onderwijskunde is een kaderstellend vak waarin
basiskennis op het gebied van onderwijzen en leren aan bod komt.
learning_objectives:
In Onderwijskunde staan de volgende leerdoelen centraal:
1. Je hebt kennis van belangrijke theorieën in relatie tot interpersoonlijk docentgedrag.
2. Je hebt kennis van belangrijke theorieën uit de adolescentiepsychologie die relevant zijn voor het onderwijs.
3. Je hebt kennis over de pedagogische opdracht van de school.
4. Je hebt kennis over de belangrijkste leer- en motivatietheorieën (en hun ontstaansgeschiedenis) en je bent in staat deze
theorieën aan elkaar en aan actuele onderwijssituaties en -ontwikkelingen te verbinden.
5. Je hebt kennis over hoe leerlingen leren, in termen van motivatie, leeractiviteiten en leeroriëntaties en je kunt deze kennis
koppelen aan de belangrijkste leertheorieën.
6. Je kunt non-verbale en verbale gedragingen van de docent waarnemen en je bevindingen schriftelijk presenteren.
7. Je kunt met behulp van het hardop-denkmethode de denkstappen en metacognitieve activiteiten van de leerlingen in kaart
brengen.
8. Je kunt een ontwikkelingsgebied van de adolescentie in kaart brengen en dit verbinden aan het lesgeven en de begeleiding van
de adolescent.
9. Je kunt een onderwijskundig onderwerp in kaart brengen en aan de hand van diverse bronnen je bevindingen schriftelijk
presenteren
